GRAND MASTER OCTOBER 18 . 1963 - OCTOB ER 16, 1964

The Ninety-Eighth Grand Master of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge, Free and Accepted M asons of the State of California. and of
the Lodges in our new S tate of Hawaii has, during his term of office
from the fall of 1963 to the fall of 1964. endeared himself to his Brethren
in this Grand Jurisdiction. He has fully obeyed the ancient injunctions
to "be a good man and true" and " to work diligently. live creditably.
and 'a ct honorably by a ll men ...
Elmer Wilson Heald was born on January 7, 1885, in Marshal
County, Kansas ..and was brought to Santa Cruz County in California
when he· was a small boy fi ve years of age. At Santa Cruz he attended
public school, the Branciforte School. The fam ily moved to Palo Alto
and Elmer attended Palo Alto H igh School, and upon his graduation
from that high school became a student at S tanford University.
Upon his graduation from Stanford he taught school for two years
in a rural school in Idaho, and thereafter enrolled in the Stanford School
of Law, graduating therefrom with the Deg ree of Doctor of Jurisprudence in 1916 .
. He served his country in two world wars, in the first W orld War
serving ·in France and Germany. He entered the army as a private and ,
when discharged at the close o f tha t war, it was as First Lieutenant.
During the second World W ar he served as Lieutenant Colonel in the
California State Reserves.

"GOD IS EVER YT HING "

of people today, God is one who does not count, or at least One who
does not matter very much.
Now then, turn for a moment, if you will to the Bible, and look at
the contrast of attitude, that we find toward God in this Holy Book.
This little library of Scripture, which contains almost every kind of
literature, was written by over a hundred authors. and it covers a period
of over a thousand years; however, it was made a single UNIT by just
one fact which can be expresse d in just two words ... GOD MATTERS! And the very first four words in the Bible give us the key to all
of it namely. "IN THE BEGINN ING GOD."
We have no science, as such, in the Bible, but when "Holy Writ"
mentions such things as those with which science now deals. it tells us
that GOD created them and owns them! The heavens and their contents,
the earth and everythin g in it, the sea and everythi ng in it, are all called
upon to praise Hi's Holy Name!
Listen to these typical sentences from our Bible. "The heavens
declare the glory of God." "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness
thereof." "The sea is His and He made it." We have splendid poetry
in the Bible, and drama and myth and legend and parable and biograph y
and prophecy, but, all of these are simply instruments to make men
realize just one thing ... that GOD MATTE RS!
We have history in the Bible, but even accuracy does not matter
to the writer as much as the desire to show the Hand of God at work
and that God Matters! The Bible concludes with the strange dreams of
a visionary. and some of it is as hard to understa nd as some modern
paintings. However , shining through it over-all is the authority of God
reigning for e~r and ever, that God really Matters. forever!
Now then, so many men have given that all up, and they seem to
act now as though God did not matter at all. They have substitut ed
man instead and they do not mean it even at Christma s when they sing
"Glory to God in the highest." For with far more sincerity and meaning
they could sing "Glory to man in the highest," for them man is the
master of things. And, my friends, you know just as well as I do, that
deep down in the hearts of so many men today, that is what they really
mean ... "Man is the master of things."
There is an old Danish fable which tells how a spider slid down a
single filament of web from the lofty timbers of the barn and establish ed
himself on a lower level of living. There he spread his web, caught flies,
grew sleek and prospere d. And then, one Sunday afternoo n, while wandering about his premises, he saw this thread that stretched up into
the dark unseen above him and thought . . . "How useless!" So, he
snapped the thread and immediately his web collapsed and soon he was
trodden under the foot of man. And you know, my .friends, I feel like
saying to you this morning with all the power I can get from GOD,
that the curse of modern life today is man's decision, that God does not
matter, that man can manage by himself, and that man is the master of

THE VERY REVEREND LESTER E. BOND, B.A., M.A., B.D., D.D.

Grand Chaplain
Most Worship ful and Members of the Grand Lodge:
I want to express my apprecia tion to Elmer Heald and to all the
officers of this Grand Lodge for the joy of one of the happiest years of
my life in serving as your Grand Chaplain this past year. Our Grand
Master has endeared himself to me as one of the grandest of Masons
and finest of men I have ever known. I would also be remiss if I did not
publicly thank Past Grand Master Joe Shell for suggestin g my name to
?ur Grand M?ster and also to Brother Ben Salmon for putting the idea
mto Joe Shells head. I was raised in the Third Degree of Masoney in
Hattiesb urg, Mississippi, in 1918. Since then, there have been many
marvelous opportunities for service in Masonry but this past year has
topped them all.
.~nasmuch as our common denomin ator in Masonry is "belief in
God and because our eyes and more particula rly our ears are always
alert to men and especially young men who express a belief in God; and
inasmuch as our Fraterni ty in Californ ia and all over America is in dire
need of increasing its ranks numerically; it therefore seems to me as I
have tried to face this problem these past months, that at least one of
our basic needs in Masonry todaiy is for each one of us to rethink and
face again our attitude and beliefs concerning God.
It is for this reason that I have read for you this morning from the
ninth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles and I would especially call your
attention to verse four where Saul raises the question: "Tell me, Lord,
who are you, and what will you have me to do?"
Let me remind you flrst of all this morning that only about sixty
percent of the populatio n of the United States are affiliated with any
Church, Protestan t, Catholic or Jewish and in about the same order.
However , on any given Sunday with the possible exception of Easter
and Christma s, we would find less than twenty-five percent of that
membership attending a service of worship.
Furtherm ore, it is generally estimate d that fewer people read their
Bibles today: and fewer people pray today with any sense that God
really matters. To be sure, there is a sort of polite, conventional, recognition of God, similar to those who would nod to one another across the
street. Or, who would talk about Santa Claus in front of a child who
still believes in Santa Claus. But, even those who admit God's existence,
seem to regard Him as a remote, impersonal and vague entity, far
removed from the life of the world. In any case, for the great majority

thing6. "lnvictus," if you please, "I am the captain of my soul." The
man who wrote those words committed suicide.
. In very fact, . th~ most terrifying and sinister thing about modern
life today, is that life 1s organized around man instead of being organized
around God. And, the real truth is, that when we try to do without God
we too, collapse! When we cut the thread that holds us in living touch
with the UNSEEN above us, we fall, and then, we too collapse! Indeed!
GOD MATTERS! God matters as air matters to our lungs. And you
~ho a~e sensitive must have already heard the choking of men, suffocat!?g with .!ear and bewilderment along with the hectic hurrying in this
rat race of men today, simply because they are trying to do without
<:7~· The assertion that "God IS" alone makes sense out of life and
hvmg tod~y. And the assertion that "God RULES," alone gives purpose
and meaning to life today or any day.
Now then, let me remind you very bluntly that "the world exists lor
God and not us." The world was created to fulfill His purposes and not
OUl'S, save as we cooperate with Him. You cannot even bend God's laws
to merely fulfill our selfish ends. Therefore, it seems to me to be so very
clear and lo~ical, that if the world was created by God for His ends
· · · then, His ends are the only ones that it will finally serve. What a
queei;,expression we sometimes use, when we talk about "breaking God's
laws. We say sometimes of a man who ignores the requirements of the
body or mind, that he has broken the laws of health. On the contrary,
the laws of, health have broken him! His condition proves it. You cannot
break Gods laws, bu~: you can be broken by defying His laws. Mr.
Ch~terton once said, If you walk to the edge of the cliff and then keep
straight on .. you do not break the law of gravity, you simply prove it."
My .friends, we should know and remember that law runs through
every !'~rt of the Universe, the physical. the psychical, the moral and
the spmtual. This very fact, you see, makes it a Universe, instead of a
Multiverse. Miracles do not give evidence of broken law, but they do
demonstrate the possibilities of law and its wealth of complexity. Yea
they point to the existence of laws we do not yet know. You see, if
miracles were the breaking of law, that very fact would then be a very
poor compliment to the wisdom of Goel, who apparently had overlOOlked
all of the possibilities which the original creation of law should have
covered. It would be as though God said to Himself, "When I made the
world, I never reckoned with such a possibility as this, now I must work
a miracle to put things right again." No indeed! Listen! No one ever
breaks God's laws!
For example, no one ever sins (which means defying a law of
~od) and gets away with it. For always there is the comeback, either
~n c~nsequences _to body, mind or soul; either in illness, or sleeplessness,
m bitter memones, or in haunting fears. Always! Forgiveness, to be
sU1'e, restores relationship to God, but it does not obliterate all of the
consequences of the sin, NOT AT ALL!

Law reigns! This is God's signature on all things, for law is created
by God. No man ever made or created a law of mathematics. He merely
discovered a law already there. The fulfillment of the discovery of a long
list of mechanical, chemical and physical laws have resulted in atomic
energiy today with all of its ramifications. But God created this marvelous
energy eons ago. You see, we merely discover the way God works, and
we call it law, but it is His law and not ours. Always His! Yea, verily.
blessed are they who learn in time that "fulness of life" is for him who
on all levels of body. mind and spirit, cooperates with the laws of God.
So, I ask you, does God matter, really? Let us consider those who
really want a better world in which to live, and in their own field are
sincerely working for it. The point I would like to make is illustrated
by a group of men who were invited to a very important dinner. After
the meal the men found that they had been invited because they were
supposed to represent various fields of endeavor, so, they were each
called upon and asked to say, how by their personal efforts the world
would be a happier place in which to live.
A scientist spoke first, but I ask you my friends, does science have
the secret of happiness? Of course we would not blame the scientists,
but their science of nuclear energy has made the world more terrified
with its atomic bombs and hydrogen bombs than it was before the
Romans landed in Britain fifteen hundred years ago. So, I ask you, must
we call this progress of science, and does it make the world happier?
Then, a medical scientist spoke of the effects of newly discovered
drugs, and I remember that in America in 1956, eight years ago, it was
reported that thirty million prescriptions for tranquilizers were used
compared to just ten million during the previous year, and I am told
that it has increased in that proportion ever since; and that the barbiturate consumption in Great Britain in 1961 averaged 24 doses per
person for every member of the population of Great Britain and Ireland.
A psychologist spoke next about analysis for everybody. Well,
knowing that a thorough examination takes around two hundred hours,
we can almost pass that one over. My personal experience in trying to
help people in the Church is that a mental patient usually waits for
weeks for an appointment. and then is lucky to get an hour once a week
and that will often be interrupted. Add to that the cost of it and •you will
see that anlysis for everybody is just impossible.
And then an educationist spoke as though the kingdom of happinese
could be found in learning. But, my friends, I have not found that university students were any happier than high school young people, have you?
In fact they are not as happy. Go to a high school football game next
week and see for yourself.
And then, a sociologist spoke about the people living in Upper
Suburbia or on the other side of the tracks, being happier than the
people living down town in the city. But, by-and-large, my experience
is that the rich are much less happy than the poor, although, of course,
if you are rich you can be very miserable with your comforts.

SPECIAL COMMIS SION ON MASON IC PRACTIC ES
Junior Past Grand Master Ira W. Coburn created this Commission
during his term as Grand Master. It was charged with the basic duty
of ascertaining from the Master Masons of this jurisdiction what the
true problems of Masonry were as viewed from their standpoin t. From
the responses received, it appears that the various suggestions presented
in the Commission's report have received substantia l support from the
constituent Lodges and have been put into practice by said Lodges.
These suggestions, among other things, include action in beginning
and ending meeting·s on time with a carefully worked out order of business; definite programs to locate, attract and bring sojourners into active
Lodge participation; the impressing upon all members of the broad areas
concerning which it is wholly permissible and appropria te to talk about
Masonry to non-members; real activity to improve the physical appearance of Lodges both inside and outside; a heavy increase in social activities, bringing the whole families of members into personal contact with
Masonry and those active in it, and the highly successful formation and
regular use of telephone committees to stimulate attendanc e at Lodge
affairs: a most determined and well planned effort to improve the leadership in all the Lodges throughou t the jurisdiction. The results attained in
all these matters have been most gratifying.
The Commission was strictly a fact finding body. In order to carry
out its mandate, a plan was devised to interview and question as large
a number of Master Masons as possible. Great numbers were interviewed and, by the use of questionnaires, large quantities of additional
material were obtained. All replies to the inquiries were held in strict

GRAND MASTE RS CONFE RENCE
Your Grand Master attended the Grand Masters Conference of
North America held in Kansas City, Missouri, on February 20, 21 and
22, 1964. Upward s of one hundred Grand Masters were present at this
Conference, representing the Grand Jurisdictions of all the States of
the Union and the Provinces of Canada. Four jurisdictions were also
represented from Europe, including Germany , Italy, France and IS!'ael.
The Grand Masters Conferen ce is governed and conducted by the Conference Committee which sets up the rules and regulations and provides
the program for the Conference. Your Grand Lodge was represen ted on
the Conferen ce Committ ee by the Grand Master o'f this jurisdiction.
This Committee also selects a Grand Master who is to preside over the
Conference and act as its chairman. The Committee chose as chairman
of the Conferen ce Most Worship ful John T. Rose, Jr., Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge of Florida. The Conferen ce Committee also selects
and appoints the members of the Time and Place Committee, consisting
of five Deputy Grand Masters. Your Deputy Grand Master Theodor e
Meriam, was selected as a member of the Time and Place Committee.
It was the consensus of opinion of the Time and Place Committee that
next year's Conferen ce should be held in Washing ton, D. C.
It is my firm belief that this Conferen ce does much to strength en
Masonry througho ut all of North America. Here in this Conferen ce the
leaders of Ma~onry in the W estem Hemisphere meet together in a
spirit of true brotherly love and cooperation in that spirit which is
expressed in the Monitor and Officers' Manual. "By the exercise of
Brotherly Love we are taught to regard the whole human species as
one family, the high and the low, the rich and the poor, who, as created
by one Almight y Parent, and inhabitants of the same planet, are to aid,
support and protect each other. On this principle Masonry unites men
of every country sect and opinion; and causes true friendship to exist
among those who might otherwise have remained at a perpetua l distance."
Much interest was displayed by the members of the Conferen ce in
the Report of the Special Commission on Masonic Practices. Our Grand
Secretar y brought a large number of copies of this report along to the
Conference which were distributed to Grand Secretaries and Grand
Masters of the several jurisdictions present. Many copies of this report
have been mailed to the other grand jurisdictions and much interest has
been displayed in what California is trying to accomplish in our Grand
Jurisdiction.

SOJOUR NERS
Your Grand ,Master has made this a major part of this Masonic Year.

It is my belief that we could add thousands of new members to our mem-

bership if we could contact a major portion of the sojourners in this
Grand Jurisdiction. The exact number of sojourners in California and
Hawaii is not known. All we have is a very vague estimate. From the
number of new people flocking into this Grand Jurisdiction from all parts
of the United States and even foreign countries, it is quite certain that
the number of sojourning Brethren would run into the thousands.
In view of this situation your Grand Master placed special emphasis
on this program. A strong committee was selected and David H. Blakelock was appointed Chairman . This Committee has been working very
hard on this difficult program.
The sojourners. in many instances, have lost their contact with
Masonry and are hesitant to make themselves known to the Masons in
the community in which they are living. Many are hungry for Masonic
intercourse and fellowship. They wait for an invitation to visit and an
assurance that the examining committee will not subject them to an inquisition. However, thousands , if met with friendship and understan ding,
will affiliate with us and become fine outstandin g additions to our
membership, bringing with them a new enthusiasm and vitality to our
Grand Lodge. One of the greatest contributions which can be made to
our Fraternity will be to rekindle the interest of these sojourner s so that
they will become a part of our Jurisdiction.
We directed the Committee on Sojourner s to develop and dissemi~
nate a progcam that would implement a statewide effort to reach the
sojourner in every Masonic District in California. Letters of instructions

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

27

and suggestions were sent out to every Lodge. In addition, individual
committeemen made many personal visitations and rendered assistance
wherever requested.
The effectiveness of any program must of course be judged by the
results accomplished by the individual Lodges. In the long run, this
program can only succeed where the Masters of each Lodge enthusiast ically and energetically pursue the search for sojourners within the
jurisdiction of their own individual Lodges. In each instance where the
Master appointed an energetic and resourceful committee and carried on
the progcam offered the results were most rewarding.

CONST ITUTIO N OBSER VANCE
Over one hundred seventy-five years ago. namely May 17, 1787, a
small group of remarkable men came together at Philadelphia to create
an effective instrument of free government for the new United States of
America. With tongue and pen they set about their tremendous task. In
less than one hundred working days they created the Constitu tion of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORN IA

29

the ~?ited States of America and projected an exP.eriment in government of the people, by th~ people and for the people which still remains
a continuous challenge to all true lovers of our great system of free
government.
It is interesting to note that many of the members of this Constitu tional Convent ion were Masons and some of its outstand ing leaders were
Master Masons. The President. George Washing ton, was a Mason and
one of its most distinguished members, Benjamin Franklin, was a
Master Mason. Little wonder, therefore, that one of our Grand Lodge
committees is designat ed as the Committee on Constitu tion Observance.
The month of Septemb er is ·s et aside for this purpose because the Constitution was signed by the members of the convention on the 17th day
of September, 1787, and was ratified on the 21st day of June, 1788, by
twelve of the thirteen colonies.
Your Committee on Constitution Observa nce has done an outstand ing job during the Masonic Year of 1964. During this year, for the first
time, there has been full coverage by radio and television all over the
State of California. This program continued through the early part of
September up to the middle of the month. It was pointed out by the
Chairma n of the Committee to the station managem ents that this program was "non-political and non-controversial." and that it was a program which the Masonic Fraterni ty has been celebrating for many years.
The result of this radio and television coverage has been a tremendous
success and has enabled the Grand Lodge of Californ ia to present its
Constitution Program s to millions of people.
City and county-wide celebrations were held througho ut the State
and were attended by thousand s of people. In the State of Hawaii, in its
capital city, Honolulu, a great mass celebration was staged in the Municipal Auditorium with an overflow audience. It is estimated that approximately eight thousand persons attended this Constitu tion Observa nce
Celebration sponsore d by the Masons of the State of Hawaii.
This has indeed been a most outstand ing Constitu tion Observa nce
for our Grand Jurisdiction and without doubt much good has been accomplished in spreadin g knowledge and respect for this invaluable document of freedom and constitutional government. Love and respect for our
Constitu tion must ever be kept alive in our great State of California and
the Fraterni ty of this State can well be proud of the program for this
Masonic Year.
It is our firm belief that the Grand Lodge Committee on Constitution
Observa nce should be made a standing committee and it is our recommendation that action be taken at this Communication to carry out this
recommendation.
In view of the importance of this program of Grand Lodge and the
accomplishments achieved this year. and to enable the incoming Grand
Master to carry on this most importan t Constitution Observa nce Month,

thi:oughout the · Grand Jurisdiction of California. During the present

DECISION No. 1
Facts:
A Lodge, acting through its Lodge Building Association, initiated a
money raising campaign with · a goal of $60,000.00. The Lodge, acting
through either its Officers or the Building Association, employed a
private company to conduct a drive to raise a portion of this money.
Lists of the members of the Lodge, members of the Eastern Star and
White Shrine were prepared and given to the company to be used for
the solicitation of this money for the Lodge.

Decision:
From the facts submitted and under the appropriate Sections of California Masonic Code, it is my opinion that there has been a violation of
our Masonic Code and the Lodge involved and the members thereof
should be so notified and all further solicitation of funds under said plan
should cease.

DECISIONS

DECISION No. 2
Facts:
A private cemetery in the City of Brea contained a section called
"Acacia Lawn ... The Grand Lecturer and an Assistant Grand Lecturer
requested an opinion as to whether or not an altar could be placed in
the "Acacia Lawn" section of ·said cemetery with a Masonic emblem
thereon and, further, asked if this altar could be dedicated by Grand
Lodge.
Decision:
It is my opinion that there i·s no violation of Masonic Law in placing
the said altar in the Acacia Lawn section and that it may have inscribed
thereon some Biblical inscription but no inscription taken from our
ritual or manual or other strictly Masonic in nature.
As to the dedication of this plot:
It is my opinion that same cannot be dedicated by Grand Lodge
because it is not a Masonic Cemetery and therefore is not entitled to a
Masonic Dedication Ceremony.

One of the most important tasks which devolves upon the Grand
Master is to apply and interpret the California Masonic Code to factual
situations presented to him by the constituent Lodges, MasteM of
Lodges, Inspectors. Grand Lodge Officers, and concordant organizations

DECISION No. 3

the present Masonic Temple building located at 350 Cedar Street, San

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

Diego. At the time of this purchase there was a bowling alley located in
the b~ement of said building. This bowling alley at the time had an "on
sale" liquor license to sell and dispense intoxicating liquor to its bowling
patrons.

Applying these Sections of the California Masonic Code to the
facts as stated in a letter addressed to the Grand Master, it appears to
be dear and certain that the sale of beer in the bowling alley in the
basement of the Masonic Temple at 350 Cedar Street in San Diego is a
violation of the Masonic Code and is definitely prohibited by all the
Sections of said Code hereinbefore quoted.
The fact that the only entrance to the bowling alley was from an
outside door and from the street, and that there was no other entrance
to said bowling alley does not take this case out of the purview of said
Sections. To hold otherwise would make it possible for every Masonic
Lodge in this Jurisdiction to partition off a portion of its Temple and
make the only enti'ance thereto from the street or alley or otherwise and
then intoxicating liquor could be sold and dispensed in Masonic Temple
property or buildings. This is dearly prohibited under our present Code.
It is my opinion that the Masonic Temple Association of San Diego
cannot allow beer or any other intoxicating liquor to be sold, dispensed
or kept in the bowling alley located in the basement of its building at
350 Cedar Street, San Diego, California. And it cannot enter into the
proposed lease agreement by which it is proposed to allow the tenant
under said lease agreement to sell, dispense and keep liquor in, on or
around said bowling alley.

In November, 1963, the owner of the bowling alley entered into a
contract to sell same to a new tenant. However, under the law, the
liquor license could not be transferred and the purchaser was required
to apply to the State Board of Equalization for an "on sale" liquor
license in his own name. It also appears that there was only one entrance
to the bowling alley, which was on the street outside of the main part
of the Temple, and there was no access to the bowling alley from any
portion of the Temple except this one outside door on Vine Street. The
Temple Association was desirous of entering into a new contract with
the new tenant who was purchasing the bowling alley and the Temple
Association desired to incorporate in the new lease a clause allowing
the tenant to obtain an "on sale" liquor license so he could sell and
dispense liquor in the bowling alley of the Masonic Temple building.
Decision:
The question involved is as to whether or not the selling of beer in
the bowling alley located in the aforesaid Masonic Temple Building's
basement would be a violation of the California Masonic Code.
Also would it be a violation of the Masonic Code for the Masonic
Temple Association to enter into the proposed oral lease agreement?
An examination of the California Masonic Code discloses the following sections which appear to bear directly on these issues:
Section 199 ( i )-"Sale of alcoholic liquor in Masonic Temple
property is prohibited under any circumstances, and a department
store leasing ground floor space may not be permitted to maintain a package liquor department."
Section 199(b)-"A lodge should not hold regular meetings in a
building also occupied by a liquor selling establishment, and it
should not purchase such a building as a meeting place unless and
at the same time the business. of selling liquor can be eliminated
from the premises."
Section ( 199 ( c )-"A Lodge may not lease and hold meetings in
a place wherein the American Legion at their meetings dispense
liquor to members under a permit from the State Board of Equalization."
Section 199 ( h )-"A Temple may not be rented to another
organization for the purpose of doing what is illegal to be done by a Masonic organization • . . "

Facts:
The Officel's of a Lodge held a meeting with the Inspector of their
Masonic Disttjct for the purpose of establishing the proflciency of said
Officers preparatory to their installation. After the meeting a dinner
was served to approximately twelve persons. The question presented
was as to whether or not the cost of this meal was a proper charge

Decision:
It is my opinion that under the facts, as stated, the cost of the
meal given to the Officers of the Lodge, the Inspector, the four coaches
and other persons whose identity is not made known, would be and is an
illegal expenditure of the Lodge Funds and the Lodge should refuse to
pay same because it is contrary to the California Masonic Code.

DEc1s10N No. 12
Facts:
This request was of a technical nature and required a construction
of Section 365 California Masonic Code. The Lodge involved was seeking to amend its by-laws with respect to its dues and a question was
raised as to the effective date of the amendment.

Decision:
From reading this Section it is clear that the said amendment did
not become effective until January 15, 1964. This being the date when
the amendment was approved by the Grand Master. Said amendment
would become operative at the start of the second quarter which would
be April 1. 1964.
All dues paid in prior to April 1, 1964 would be on the basis of the
Section of the By-Laws as it existed prior to that date.
DEc1sION No. 13

Facts:
An opinion was requested as to whether or not the cost of a trowel
provided by some Lodges to be given to a Candidate in the Third Degree
could be charged to the general funds of the Lodge.
Dedsion:
A reading of those Sections of the California Masonic Code having
to do with basic laws on use of Lodges' funds. namely, Sections 409, 410,
411 and 412 do not disclose any authority for the expenditure of monies
from the general funds of the Lodge for the purchase of trowels.
There is no general program or law directing or authorizing a gift of
a trowel to the Candidate as a program of the Grand Lodge.
It is my opinion that the expenditure of money from the general funds
of the Lodge for a trowel, as a gift to the Candidate, is not authorized by
the California Masonic Code and same would be an illegal expenditure
of said funds.
DEc1s10N No. 14
Facts:
The Pharaoh of the Supreme Pyramid of the Ancient Egyptian
Order of Sciots, requested an opinion on the following: This organization, which requires as a pre-requisite to membership therein that a man

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

43

be a Master Mason, proposed to hold a social meeting in a hall which
belongs to the American Legion in which the Legion has a bar and would
serve and dispense intoxicating liquor therein. The question presented
was as to whether or not the Sciots could hold such a meeting in this hall.
Decision:
Section 199 ( g) of the California Masonic Code reads as follows:
"A Lodge may hold social or ,similar meetings in a building where
intoxicating liquor is sold over a bar, and a Mason may belong to
an organization ·r equiring Masonic membership as a prerequisite,
which holds such meetings in such buildings."
The meeting which the Sciots propose to hold as set forth above is
to be a building belonging to the American Legion, an organization
which does not require as a prerequisite to membership therein, that
a person must be a Master Mason. Under the provisions of said section
it is my opinion that the Sciots may hold their meeting in the American
Legion Hall.
DEc1s10N No. 15
Facts:
The Master and a Past Master of a Lodge submitted a written
request to change the name of said Lodge and requested a dispensation
from the Grand Master to make such a change.
Decision:
A Lodge cannot change its name by an amendment to its by-laws, or
by any other action. Likewise the name cannot be changed by a dispensation from the Grand Master. A Lodge desiring to change its name must
present the same by proper resolution to the Grand Lodge at its next
Annual Communication. Such resolution must be prepared and filed with
the Grand Secretary ninety days ( 90) prior to October 12, 1964.
DEc1s10N No. 16
Facts:
An Inspector requested an opinion on the following: In an application for the degrees of Masonry an applicant stated that when he was
seventeen years old he was charged with a felony (<Statutory rape) in
a petition filed in the Juvenile Court and was committed to the Preston
School of Industry by the Juvenile Court. The question was as to
whether or not this application could be received. The facts indicate that
the applicant at the time of commission of the offense was a minor person.
Under the Juvenile Court Law of the State of California the Juvenile
Court is not considered as a criminal court and the proceedings therein
are deemed to be in the nature of a civil proceeding, the ultimate objective
being to rehabilitate the youth involved.
Decision:
The application may be received from this applicant. As indicated

minor person, under the age of eighteen years, and by virtue of the
provisions of said law he was committed to the California Youth Authority. He was released on parole and has reinstated himself as a good
citizen in the community where he now lives and is eligible to apply for
membership in a Masonic Lodge.

DEc1s10N No. 17
Facts:
A Lodge requested permission to place a directional sign at the corner
of two streets in the city in which it was located, the sign to contain
the words "Masonic Temple" with an arrow pointing in the direction
in which the Temple is located.

· Decision:
It is true that at the 1963 Communication the Grand Master held
"I can see no sound reason why a Lodge should not be prohibited from
notifying the public, generally, of its name, number and street address
so that a weary brother Mason should perchance pass by that way he
would be informed that brother .Masons dwelt in that Community and
he would find them or their Lodge if he so desired. Also, such practice
would give notice to the public. generally. that there was a Masonic
Lodge in that community." This Decision No. 4, of the Grand Master,
came before the Committee on Jurisprudence for a recommendation to
Grand Lodge as to rejection or approval. In its report the Committee
on Jurisprudence stated: "This decision holds that it is permissible for
Lodges to display signs at entrances to towns where Lodges are located
bearing the Square and Compass emblem, names and numbers and
addresses of Lodges, dates and hour of meeting."
The Committee gave four reasons why this decision of the Grand
Master should be rejected and recommended a no vote. A majority of
Grand Lodge voted no.
In view of the facts herein set forth that all that is being requested
by the Lodge is a directional arrow indicating the direction in which
the Temple is located. It is my opinion that this in no way violates
Sections 333 (a) to ( k) of the California Masonic Code, and is not
violative of the recommendation and finding of the Committee on Jurisprudence.
It is therefore my opinion and decision that a Masonic Lodge may
erect a directional sign consisting of the words "Masonic Temple" and
an arrow indicating the direction in which the Temple is located.
DEc1s10N No. 18
Facts:
The Master of a Lodge asked for an opinion on the following state-

45

Decision:
Section 511 ( g) of the California Masonic Code reads as follows:
"One who has served a term in the state prison is not under the
tongue of good report, and it is not proper to receive his application."
Under the provision of this section it was proper for the Master of
the Lodge to refuse the application and return same together with the
check to the applicant.
One who has been convicted of a felony (robbery) and has served
a term therefore, in prison and has not received a full pardon is not
eligible to petition for the degrees of Masonry. His petition should not
be read in Lodge, but should be returned by the Master to the petitioner.

This decision covers the same factual situation as that set forth
in Decision No. 11 and your Grand ,Master held that a Masonic Temple
cannot be leased to any organization where such organization proposes
or requests the right to serve intoxicating liquor therein. Since the illegal
lease was terminated by the lessee it was ordered that the lease deposit
be returned by the lessor.

not considered as criminal in nature, but as held by our Supreme Court
"they are in the nature of a proceeding for the appointment of a guardian.

certain facts were set forth concerning the removal of a handmade model
of a sailing ship from over the Preparation Room door of the Lodge
Room of Redondo Lodge No. 328.
On June 30, 1964 a letter concerning the same subject was received
from Donald G. Campbell. the Grand Lecturer. In substance the factual
situation presented is as follows:
Redondo Lodge had a handmade model of a sailing ship placed
over the door leading from the Preparation Room into the Lodge
Room. The Grand Lecturer requested the Lodge to remove same.
It was removed. Some members of the Lodge evidently questioned
the authority of the Grand Lecturer to order its removal. The
Grand Lecturer has requested an opinion.
This matter was presented to Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication in 1957 by two Resolutions. One presented by three
Lodges jointly and one by El Segundo Lodge No. 507.
These Resolutions referred to the use of Charts, Ships and Slides
and required the Ritual Committee "to re-evaluate the entire
ritual of the fi11st three degrees with a view to recommend the reintroduction of the 'chart' and re-granting permission to display
a model of a boat near the door of the Preparation Rooms."
These resolutions were referred to three committees. Jurisprudence. Policy and General Purposes and Ritual.
At the Annual Communication in 1958 Reports were made by a
Special Committee on the use of visual aids. One was designated
a majority report and the other the minority report.
The majority report was to the effect that so called visual aids
should not be used.
The minority report recommended the appointment of a new
Committee to report to Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication. The minority report was adopted. A new committee
was appointed to report to the next annual communication.
In 1959 this Special Committee made a long and detailed report
to Grand Lodge which was adopted in full.
This report recommended that any slide, ship, map, chart. or picture of any nature. showing in part or in whole, the work of the
three degrees of Masonry is contrary to the laws of the fraternity
and in violation of the obligation of the order. and no Lodge in
this jurisdiction shall use such equipment in any way, nor shall
any Mason be in possession thereof.
The Committee went on to state "we can see no reason for a
change in the presentation and lecture of the three degrees as
now constituted."
This would appear to be the final word of Grand Lodge on this
subject. As indicated above the report of the Committee was
adopted by Grand Lodge.

DECISION No. 21
Facts:
An opinion was 1'equested as to whether or not an applicant in
filling out his application form could print all of the answers and matters
required rather than write same in his own handwriting.
Decision:
Section 526 only specified that "applications for the degrees and for
affiliation shall be in writing."
The applicant may fill out the application if he so desires by printing
the required answers and information thereon, but, he must sign his
name in his own handwriting: he cannot print his signature.
DECISION No. 22
Facts:
A Lodge Auditing Committee refused to approve a bill covering
what appeared to be its share of expenses in a joint enterprise for a
"Masonic Sunrise Service" in March, 1964, on the grounds that it was
not a proper charge against Lodge funds. The facts as to the origin of
the bill are not set forth in the inquiry respecting the propriety of its
payment.

Decision:
Sections 409, 410, 411and412 seem to govern the use and disbursement of Lodge funds.
A careful reading of these sections and the annotations thereto disclose no authorization for this expenditure of this bill as submitted to
the Secretary. The annotations under Sections 409 and 412 indicate that
this is not a proper charge against Lodge funds.
It is my opinion and decision that the auditing committee was justified in refusing to approve this bill.

DE MoLAY WEEK

March 16th to 20th, 1964
The Youth of today are the Citizens of tomorrow. Today we find
the enemies of our Country seeking to undermine our future by capturing
the minds of our youth. Those who would destroy us are devoting their
time and money to an effort to control the thinking of our young people
and to poison their minds against our beloved country.
Today one of the most disturbing factors throughout our nation is
the amount of unrest displayed by the Youth of America. Juvenile problems have more than doubled during the last five years, and have now
reached an all-time high. The decline in spiritual and moral values of a
considerable segment of our younger generation is.a problem of major
importance.
The great Order of De Molay offers Masonry a tremendous opportunity to combat these evil forces. De Malay is a mighty asset in build--ing character into the lives of its members. Let us not waste any precious
time in giving our active support to this Masonic youth organization.
By this work we can assure a bright future for our Country and for
Freemasonr y.
Too many of our Lodges are not yet aware that Grand Lodge has
sanctioned support of De Molay. Section 333f of the California Masonic
Code records Grand Lodge approval of the ideals, aims and purposes of
the Order of De Malay.
The opening ceremonies of each De Malay Chapter includes an
avowal of support for our country, our public schools, and the church
of one's choice, and respect for the home and all it stands for.
In recognition of the lifetime of values in this fine youth organization, in the hope that more Lodges will undertake to sponsor and
support De Malay Chapters in their communities, I hereby proclaim
the week of March 16th to 20th to be De Molay Week. Each Lodge is
directed to give due notice of this Proclamatio n in its March bulletin.
It is also my direction that this Proclamation be read at the February
and March Stated Meetings.
Dated: January 15, 1964
Fraternally yours,
Attest:

The founders of our nation recogniz ed that freedom and self-government could only be achieved and maintain ed by a people educated in
the techniqu e of self-gove rnment and informed on the ways and mea ns
of preservin g their freedom .
The Constitu tion of the United States proclaim ed those fundame ntal precepts of governm ent essential to the preserva tion of the freedom
and dignity of the individua l. The America n concept of universa l free
public educatio n, which began to develop not long after the signing of
the Constitu tion, provided the only satisfact ory means of achieving the
goals set by our Constitution.

care of the progress ive State; and that upon our Public Schools depends

govern , to assume responsibility is greater than ever.

and the Public Schools by exercisin g our duty as citizens every day of

Public School Observa nces.

officials. administ rators and teachers. We can urge public officials to issue
Public Schools Week proclama tions.
I direct that only Stated Meeting s or those for Public Schools vVeek

CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

At a few times in the over-all history of mankind, we seem to reach
certain high points in time, whene men are afforded the opportunity to
rise to great heights, meet the challenges of the times, and produce for
all posterity certain fundamental and everlasting concepts. Such a time
in history occurred during the Revolutionary War era, out o f which
emerged the Constitution of the United States, on September 17, 1787.
It was, and is, an ever-modern and living document, which contains
such basic, non-controversial and undeniably true principles for the
regulation of the conduct of man to man, that, if preserved, the freedom
and dignity of the individual American is forever secured. This is accomplished by the establishment of government under law, as opposed
to government by men, and by securing to each of us certain individual
basic rights under the law, which rights are as valuable today as they
were sought after by man before this great document was produced.
The tragic assassination of last November points up the undeniable
propriety of government by law, not by men, when the continuity of government was so graphically demonstrated at that time. However. this is
but a narrow application of the timeless truths contained in this document.
My Brethren , let us remember that men enjoy freedom only while
they are willing to fight for it, and if need be. to die for it, a nd are
vigilant to any deterioration in the form of that freedom . Let our
motto be:
"The Price of Liberty is Eternal Vigilance"
This observance should be planned to arouse community spirit and
interest. open to the public and sponsored by Lodges or districts or
both in conjunction with other organizations when or where this will
help in making the observance a complete success.
I therefore proclaim September 1964 to be Constitution Observance
Month, a nd direct every Lodge in this jurisdiction to commemorate our
Constitution with a public observance held on a date as close as possible
to the Anniversary date of September 17th.
The Proclamation shall be read at Stated Meetings during the
months of July and August 1964.
Dated : June 19, 1964
Sincerely and Fraternally yours,
Attest :
EDWARD H. SIEMS

ELMER W. HEALD

Grand Secretary

Grand Master

TO ALL CONSTITUENT LODGES
CHAIN LETTERS

A flood of chain letters has reached the office of the Grand Secretary.
Sending out chain letters or continuing a chain letter is a violation of
postal regulations.
Section 124.55 of the Postal Manual on non-mailable matter
reads
"Any libelous, scurrilous. defamatory or threatening language
whether written or printed or which by its manner or style of·
display is obviously intended to reflect injuriously on the character or conduct of another."
As good citizens we should be above this sort of practice. I am certain many who participate are not aware of the possible penalties involved. It could result in fine or imprisonment or both.
In order that all Masons are aware of this violation, it is requested
that this notice be read at the next Stated Meeting of your Lodge
following its rece4pt and that a notice be included in your next trestleboard.
A continuation of the practice of sending "chain letters" will be
deemed a violation of this order of the Grand Master and will be dealt
with accordingly.
Fraternally yours.
ELMER

w. HE.ALO

Grand Master
Attest :
EDWARD H . SIEMS

Grand Secretary

MASONIC PLAQUE OR SIGN WITH EMBLEM
AT ENTRANCE TO CITY
(6)
To the M ost W orshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it is in the spirit of M asonry to broaden the universality of its a¢peal. and
WHEREAS, such spirit can be manifest by a public gesture of
welcome to Master Masons who are visiting or moving to a new loca l~
ity in the jurisdiction in which a duly established Masonic Lodge (or
Lodges) exists. and
WHEREAS. it would be helpful to visitors to know the time, date,
and location of the Stated Meetings of such local Lodges,
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED:
1. That Section 333-S of the M asonic Code be rescinded.
2. Any duly constituted Masonic Lodge, operating under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of the State of California , individuaHy or
jointly with other Masonic Lodges in the same District or geographica l
area, may erect. or cause to be erected, an outdoor sign bearing M asonic
insignia . containing details as to meetings. and extending a welcome to
Master Masons to attend.
3. The Inspector ( s) concerned, acting as a representative of Grand
Lodge, will satisfy himself (themselves) that the location of any such
sign (preferably at the geographical limits of a city or town) and
quality (sufficiently durable to maintain a good appearance under all
weather condWons) are appropriate to a favorable public impression

of the Masonic Fraternity. and. also . that all legal requirements have

WHEREAS. the California Masonic Code prohibits the publication in trestle boards of the names of candidates and the times when
they are to receive their degrees; and
WHEREAS, such publication is permitted in many other jurisdictions in the interests of their Lodges and their candidates; and
WHEREAS, the trestle boards of Lodges are circulated only among
members of the particular Lodges and such other brethren as may be
properly entitled to receive the same: and
WHEREAS. the publication of the na mes of candidates and the
dates when they will receive their degrees will stimulate interest in
Masonry and will increase Lodge attendance,
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that the Lodges be
permitted to publish in their respective trestle boards the names of their
candidates and the dates when they are to receive their various degrees
and accordingly that sections 518-e and 334-g of the California Masonic Code be repealed .
Respectfully submitted.
MAURICE A . HARBAND, M .. No. 120
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General Purposes.

PUBUSH NAMES OF ELECTED CANDIDA TES
(7)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
WHEREAS, the Master of San Diego Lodge No. 35 has appointed
a Committee on Masonic Practices which has met on several occasions
and discussed various problems including that of attendance of members during degrees, and
WHEREAS, the members of said committee unanimously believe
that increased attendance at the conferral of degrees may be aq:omplished by permitting the candidates' names to be printed in Lodge bulletins and sent to the Lodge's members through the U. S. Mail.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 334 CMC be
amended to add the following words at the end of said section:
"A Lodge shall have the authority to inform its members by U. S.
Mail in the Lodge bulletin or otherwise of the names of applicants for
the degrees and it shall have the authority to so inform its members as
to the names of candidates and the dates of conferral of the several
degrees."
Respectfully submitted,
JAMES H. LEACH. P.M .. No. 35

SOLICITATION OF CERTAIN ADVERTISING
(9)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. Section 334 of the C.M .C. provides that "No Lodge,
or member of a Lodge. shall solicit, sponsor. insert, place or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication. which purports
to be Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for
any body, order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership" ; and
WHEREAS , the medium of advertising is an acknowledged method
of informing persons of honorable and free enterprise: and
WHEREAS. the loss of respectable revenue has so limited the
financial ability of Masonic bodies to publicize or carry on their good
works that Masonry has substantially suffered: and
WHEREAS, churches or places of holy worship have recognized
that individuals who are made familiar with the value of good products
through the medium of advertising and are the mutual recipients of
substantial benefits;
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 334 be amended
to read :
No Lodge, or member of a Lodge. shall solicit, sponsor, insert,
place or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication that might bring discredit to the good name of Masonry or prove

70

to be less than beneficial to any person who might be influenced to
attend, use or purchase the items so advertised.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED. th at all other references contained in our laws, rules, regulations, edicts, decisions, or any other
ma tter on this subject, written or unwritten, having the force of law
which are contrary hereto are rescinded.
Respectfully submitted.

VA RIED INITIATION FEE
(11)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. it is in the interest of our noble and ancient craft to
encourage young men to petition for entrance into the fraternity; and.
WHEREAS, the report of the Special Commission on Masonic Practices indicated a constantly falling ratio of Masonic membership to
general population; and.
WHEREAS. the same commission reported (on page 7) that young
men between the ages of 21 and 30 petition for entrance in relatively
small numbers; and,
WHEREAS. The Most Worshipful Grand Master in his message
to the Craft in the Spring 1964 California Freemason urges that thought

73

be given to attracting young men to membership in the fraternal organization,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the following
paragraph shall be added to Section 552 of the California Masonic
Code:
The maximum fee which a Lodge may levy for conferring the three
degrees on young men between the ages of 21 years and 31 years shall
not exceed a total of $50.00.
Respectfully submitted,

GRAND MASTER'S DECISION NO. 7
(12)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, at the time Section 408 of the C.M.C. was made law.
its subject matter was prohibited by the laws of the United States of
America; and ·
WHEREAS, the passing of time has brought about a change in the
law and opinion of proper social and moral conduct in relation to the
serving and consumption of spiritous, malt or fermented liquors; and
WHEREAS, decisions of Grand Masters over the years have been
based on this section that may prove to be obsolete thus making them
contradictory to the Fraternal and Membership interest; and
WHEREAS, it is obvious that restraint be exercised on some occasions and in certain places but that the intent should be confined to
Masonic Temples and regular Blue Lodge Meetings as well as the concordant bodies of Masonry;
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that a committee be appointed by the Grand Master for the purpose of making a study of Section
408 of C.M.C., to recommend amendment where proper and to make
clear the intent and authority of this section over organizations not considered concordant or properties whose title is not held by Grand Lodge
or its concordant bodies; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Decision No. 7 of Grand
Master Elmer Heald relating to the above be not ratified but held in

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

abeyance until such time as the results of the special committee be made
available and/or adopted.

EXPENDITURE LODGE FUNDS TO CHARTER
CHAPTER OF ORDER OF DeMOLAY
(14)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. the Report of the Special Commission on Masonic
Practices in 1963 which was ordered under the direction of Past Grand
Master Ira W. Coburn reported that 91 o/o of all Masons queried were
strongly in favor of broadening and expanding the present permissive
areas for the financial assistance of both boys' and girls' youth groups;
and
WHEREAS. the California Masonic Code section 41 le and 412u
states, " Lodge funds may not be used in connection with the sponsoring
of the Order of DeMolay"; and
WHEREAS. Lodges are allowed to purchase equipment for presentation to new Lodges and Cornerstones for Cornerstone Ceremonies;
where can a more appropriate cornerstone be laid than of sponsoring
the Order of DeMolay.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED. that Section 41le and 412u
be amended by the addition of the following: "Except for the necessary
fee established by the Supreme Council Order of DeMolay for Chartering a Chapter of the Order of DeMolay."
Respectfully submitted.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
(16)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
WHERE,AS. the custom of refusing a dmission to a physically imperfect applicant came to be developed during the old days of operative
Masonry. when the work on the erection of stone edifices was both
arduous and hazardous. and a physically impaired workman constituted
a da nger to hims elf and to his fellow workers, and liable to become a
burden to his Lodge or Guild, and
WHEREAS . we no longer work in operative Masonry but speculative only. these physical requirements are now obsolete, and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California possesses legislative
powers w hich extend to every case of legislation not expressly delegated
by itself to the Lodges. The Constitution, Regulations and Uniform
Code of By-Laws for Lodges, which the Grand Lodge has an inalienable
right to adopt and promulgate at its own convenience, and to alter.
amend, or repeal at its own pleasure. limited only by a strict adherence
to the Ancient Landmarks of the Order. are final and binding upon all
Lodges and Masons within its jurisdiction until so al tered, amended , or
repealed.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, tha t Section 512 (not including sub-paragraphs a to j inclusive) of the California Masonic Code be
amended as follows:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"512. Sound discretion required. The question as to the physical
sufficiency of the Applicant shall be left to the sound discretion of the
Lodge. When the applicant is unable to comply literally with the physical
requirements, the Master shall state the nature and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before ballot is taken. The loss of the left forearm
would not constitute physically disqualifying an applicant for the degrees
of Masonry. (Former RD. Sec. 209.)"

EXTEND ST A TEWIDE TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION
TO ALL LODGES
(17)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
The purposes of this resolution are to extend statewide territorial
jurisdiction to a ll Lodges and to eliminate the I 0 mile limit and the
requirement for waiver of jurisdiction. The present procedure on waiver
causes delay by requiring that an application be processed through two
different Lodges when the Lodge receiving the application. through
proper diligence, could safely investigate the applicant. Also, modern
travel and communication facilities reduce the hazards of distance. so to
compel a prospective applicant to seek membership in a Lodge wit hin
I 0 miles of his residence, when he perhaps knows not one member, is
not conducive to membership increase about which we are concerned
today. Nor, does an active, virile Lodge need protecting by exclusive
jurisdiction.
To effect the purposes of this resolution will require many changes
in our Code.
We therefore present the following:
RESOLVED: That Sections of the California Masonic Code be
amended , as follows:
Sec. 517- Strike the words" ... and within the jurisdiction of the
Lodge during six months . . . "
Sec. 518-Repeal.
Sec. 519-Repeal.
Sec. 522- Repeal.
Sec . 524-Repeal.
Sec. 527-6-Strike the words " ... and the place above named more
than six months .. .''
RESOLVED. further, that the Code Commission be directed to
eliminate, in whole or in part, all annotations under the foregoing sec-

c.

CONCURRENT JURISDICTION AND PUBLICATION
(18)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. the custom to promote interest and good fellowship
among the Lodge brethren and candidates for degrees are extremely
important in this present day and age, and
WHEREAS. many Blue Lodge Brothers have been denied the
opportunity to participate in their friends ' degrees due to present communications within their respective Lodges,
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED . that Section 518 (not including sub-paragraph s a to f inclusive) of the California Masonic Code
be amended as follows:
" 518. Concurrent jurisdiction. If two or more Lodges are located
within the corporate limits of any city, town , or place they shall have
concurrent jurisdiction therein. Any of them can receive and act on the
application for degrees of residents thereof or persons residing nearer
thereto than to any other place where a Masonic Lodge exists . Each of
such Lodges has separate jurisdiction over its own members. and concurrent jurisdiction over all Masons not members of one of them. who
reside in such city, tQ'..vn or place, or nearer thereto than to any other
place where a Lodge exists. and each shall within ten days after receipt
of an application by the Lodge notify such other Lodge or Lodges of
any application it may receive for degrees or affiliation and waiver of
jurisdiction. That it is within the Lodge's discretion to publish the name
of candidates for the date of conferring of the Fellowcraft and Master
Mason degree in their respective Lodge bulletin. ( 1962) (Former R. D.
Sec. 214. )"
Respect£ ully submitted,

LIMIT PROMISE IN QUESTION 15 TO PROFICIENCY
(19)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California requires as a part of
Section 527 of the C.M.C. (Form of Application for Degrees) under
Question No. 15 the following:
"Do you promise that you will not apply for or receive any
degree or be initiated in any Lodge, Order or organization the
prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master
Mason, until you have given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge, that you are entirely proficient and wellqualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason
and in no event within twelve months after you have received the
Degree of Master Mason?" and
WHEREAS. the portion which reads, "and in no event within
twelve months after you have received the Degree of Master Mason."
was designed for the purpose of retaining the newly raised brother's
interest and attendance in his Blue Lodge; and
WHEREAS. it has not a<:complished its purpose but has in fact
allowed a period of Masonic inactivity during which time our brethren
have turned to other interests and grown further away from their
Masonic involvement; and
WHEREAS. it i-s believed that voluntary activity promoted by an
attractive program as well as the cooperation of all Masonic bodies one
with another. will better serve our Masonic purpose;
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 527 be amended
to delete from Question No. 15 the words "and. in no event within twelve
months after you have received the Degree of Master Mason?" and
shall hereafter read:
Do you promi·s e that you will not apply for or receive any
degree or be initiated in any Lodge. Order or organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master
Mason, until you have given satisfactory evidence. by strict examination in open Lodge. that you are entirely proficient and wellqualified in the Candidate's Lecture of Master Mason?
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED. that all other references contained in our laws. rules. regulations, edicts, decisions, or any other
matter on this subject, written or unwritten, having the force of law.
which are contrary hereto are rescinded.
THOMAS E. p ARSONS,
P.M., No. 736
WALTERS. PoTTs. P.M .. No. 35

intimately familiar with M asonic law and custom, and
WHERE AS. on occasion , our brethren , who serve in official capacities in these youth organiza tions, have, inadverte ntly, caused embarrassment to the craft, or have presente d an unfavora ble public image.
and
WHERA S. is it desirable that organiza tions associate d in the public
mind with Masonry should be under closer supervisi on of Grand Lodge.
THERE FORE BE IT RESOL VED that Section ··-····· be added to
C.M.C. as follows:
No M ason shall hold office in any capacity in any youth organiza tion
wherein the prerequis ite is that he be a Master Mason. except that he
shall have presente d himself before the Inspecto r of the District in whose
jurisdicti on the meeting place of said youth organiza tion lies, and satisfy
said Inspector as to his proficiency in the C.M.C. and in our ancient
usages and cus toms, to the extent that his incumben cy in such position
shall bring no discredit or embarras sment to the craft.

(29)
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHERE AS . the Preamble is presently being given from the East
by the Chaplain while the Senior Deacon conducts the Candidate . and
WHERE AS . in years past it was common practice to have the Preamble given by either the Chaplain from the East or by the Senior
Deacon as he conducted the Candidate , and
WHERE AS, the Candidate receives a more direct delivery and the
Senior Deacon has a better opportuni ty to time his proper arrival at the
South when he himself does the talking, and
WHEREA S, some Lodges have a permanen t Chaplain and the
knowledg e of this discourage s the Junior Officers from learning the
Preambles . and
WHERE AS. this resolution proposes no changes in floor work or
in wording but only the advantage s of either method of delivery which
a Lodge may prefer, now th erefore
BE IT RESOLV ED . that the Senior Deacon be permitted to give
the Preamble from the floor w hile conductin g the Candidate , or that the
Chaplain deliver it from the East. The choice of either to be at the
discretion of the Master.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
On May 21. 1964 this Grand Lodge suffered a great loss in the
passing of our then Grand T reasurer , Past Grand Master Arthur
Melvin Warren. Suitable memorial services will be acknowledged at
the scheduled time.
Our Grand Master. Most Worshipful Elmer W. Heald , prevailed
upon me to succeed to this higher responsibility. I wish to express publicly my appreciation to him for this opportunity for further service to
this great Fraternity of ours.
Attached will be found all of the financial reports and audits of
Grand Lodge, Masonic Hornes of California and the California Masonic
Memorial Temple. It was my pleasure to sit in with members of the office
staff. and the auditors. Lybrand Ross Bros. & Montgomery. in reviewing
the detail and the work that went into these audits. These statements
are meaningful. I sincerely hope that each Lodge officer will study them
carefully. Only then will you appreciate how your dollars have been
spent. Detailed records and vouchers are on file in the office of the Grand
Secretary. Our professional Auditors have carefully reviewed all appropriations and disbursements as provided in Section 194 C.M.C.
At this point I wish to commend them for their careful attention to
detail. My immediate predecessor was. at the time of his untimel y death,
in the process of re-evaluating with the Grand Secretary the office procedures with particular reference to control and methods. I have tried to
carry on from where his work was interrupted. Part of the study was
built around recent procedural changes being anticipated by the Grand
Secretary and his staff.
There has been added to the staff Brother Ray Halloway, a man
well trained and experienced in all phases of accounting procedure.
Under his able direction a number of innovations have been made in office
procedure and record keeping. A new Burroughs book-keeping machine
has been installed.
Other innovations are being studied. A s your Grand Treasurer it
shall be my purpose to keep in close touch with these timely developments. It is entirely possible that after some experimenting it may be
desirable to make certain recommendations which could further facilitate the over all program of record keeping. auditing. and so forth. Such
recommendations would only be forthcoming a fter careful consideration
and consultation with all interested parties such as our C.P.A.'s, the
Chairman of our Finance Committee, the Grand Master. and others.

complied with by Jonathan Lodge No. 545 and Veritas Lodge No. 640
they consolidat ed, effective December 3, 1963, with the approval of

No. 550 they consolidat ed. effective December 5. 1963, with the approval
of the Grand Master. The Lodge will be known as King Solomon·s
Seaport Lodge No. 260, located at San Francisco.
The Grand Secretary requests authority to properly endorse these
Charters.

For the past two years we have discussed suspension, of members
for non-payment of dues and the remission of members dues. I am
pleased to say that both have decreased during the las t yea r. Although
the decreases are slight in both categories, the efforts made have resulted
in progress in the right direction. Congratulation s are due the Masters
and the Lodges.
Suspensions for Non-Payment of Dues
.
.
f
The strength of Masonry is not in its numbers. It 1s. the quality o
the applicant that counts. "ls he worthy and well qualified? Does he
come of good report?"
1
It is conceivable that the Lodge which consistently suspend~ a re_atively high percentage of its members for non-payment of dues 1s saymg
to itself. in effect, "Perhaps a poor investigation was made of that brother
in the first instance."

101

Analysis of the suspension of members for non-payment of dues
shows a decrease of 30 over last year. However, it is evident that there
is still much room for improvement. In reviewing the action taken by
the Lodges, in this respect, we find that of the I 401 total suspensions
for the 1963-64 period 142 lodges have been responsible for 943. I n
other words, approximately 20% of our Lodges have made 67 % o f the
total suspensions for non-payment of dues. Further review discloses that
one Lodge of almost I 000 members has , during the past five years.
suspended 68 of its members. This is approximately 7% of its total
membership! Still more alarming is the fact that several other smaller
Lodges have each suspended for non-payment of dues 1 I % of their
membership during the same five year period.
Frankly, many of our Lodges have been complacent with respect
to such suspensions. It is the easy thing to do, exerting no effort, to say,
"Why should I worry about the other fellow-my dues are paid-let
him worry about himself." The result is SUSPENSIO N and loss of
membership-p utting another Mason "on the shelf." Remember that
over 7200 Masons have actually been put on that shelf during the past
five years. and only 1800 have found their way back into active membership. Here is a prospective field of approximately 5400 Masons-many
of whom, if personally contacted, might return to active participation.
If all of these members could be convinced to return to active membership, it would mean an annual increased revenue to our Lodges of over
$85,000. Remember also, Brethren , that it is legal to solicit these members to return to active membership.
We wish to recommend to the Masters and incoming Officers of
the Lodges that a concerted effort be made to decrease the number of
suspensions for non-payment of dues. This can be accomplished by
appointing a full time "Delinquent Dues Committee," such to be in
keeping with the size of the Lodg~ne which is active and will function twelve months of each year working closely with the Master and
the Secretary. As an example, may I cite one of our largest Lodges
which has employed this type of program. Its record is outstanding!
This Lodge has a membership in excess of I 000, yet in the past three
years the suspensions have totaled only 12 members. Try it, Brethren ,
a full time "Delinquent Dues Committee" DOES work!
Advance Dues Remissions
A survey of the question of advance remission of dues shows that.
while there was a slight decrease during the last year, the number is
still large. There were 1534 advance dues remission cases for the 1963-64
period. We find that I 06 Lodges remitted dues in advance to 5 or more
of their members, and these 106 Lodges are responsible for advance
dues remissions for 11 84 of the total 1534 cases. Reduced to percentages these figures show that 15% of our Lodges account for 78 % of
the dues which were remitted in advance.

102

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Typical of the situations which have developed is one Lodge with
a membership of approximately 600 which, last 'Year, remitted dues in
advance to over 9% of its total membership. Several smaller Lodges
also remitted dues in advance for between l 0 and 13 percent of their
total membership. It appears that some Lodges have adopted the policy
of automatically remitting the dues in advance of the member who has
been a Mason 40 years or reaches the age of 75. Such a policy is contrary to our Law, and we ask that you review C.M.C. Section 577-h.
Attainment of either of these qualifications is not sufficient, because the
Law provides that dues may be remitted in advance ONLY in those
marginal cases where there may be ability to pay but where such payment would work a hardship. Further. the allowance made for "distinguished service" to the Lodge by such a member could not reasonably
be stretched to include all of the I 534 members granted advance dues
remission.
May we suggest that you analyze each advance dues remission case
carefully as to the actual eligibility for such consideration. Also, before
the seemingly illegal policy mentioned above becomes a practice of your
Lodge, study your .financial situation. Each member whose dues are
remitted must be carried by the members paying dues. Remember once
the policy of dues remission is established it is most difficult to rescind.
Excessive ·r emissions could mean a heavy .financial loss to the Lodge.
Dues remissions for the past .five years have cost our Lodge in excess
of $275,000 in loss of revenue. To be a member of a Masonic Lodge is
a great honor. To support the activities of the Lodge by the payment
of dues is not only a responsibility but it is also a privilege.

Summary
These are areas which we feel are worthy of your serious consideration and constructive action. Not only are certain of these practices
apparent violation of our regulations, but their effect on other Lodges
who have attempted to observe the intent of the Law has been negative.
In cases where suspensions for non-payment of dues are heavy remissions of dues in advance are often also heavy.
Particular notice should be taken of the fact that we have avoided
any remarks about the validity of the remission of accrued dues. This
is a matter for the discretion of the Lodges. Judgment of such ca ses, as
far as we know, is valid and justified. You will note in our discussion
of suspension of members for non-payment of dues and advance remission of dues we have not identified the particular Lodges to avoid embarrassment, but we will furnish individual Lodge records to those entitled
to the information.

To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:

The duties of the G ra nd Lecturer as set forth in Section 156 of the
Ordinances require him "to supervise and direct the A ssista nt G ran d
Lecturers in the performance of their duties. and to require conformity
with the adopted ritua l and work." The Assistant Grand Lecturer is
"to examine and instruct the Inspectors within his division in the performance of their duties. and to exercise general supervision over their
work in the Lodges under their care .. .. "
It may be readily apparent from th is excerpt that the Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand Lecturers have, throu gh the Inspectors
of the Districts, responsibility not only for the ritual work of the Grand
Lodge. but also for the supervision of. and leadership in , each District.
This, a devoted and dedicated Inspector s hould give.
The year just closed shows, in the repor ts of the Inspectors, continued progress toward the goal of meaningful service by our Lodges;
service not only to the membership of ea ch Lodge itself. b :1t service
also to our great charity, the Masonic H omes, to our Memorial Temple
and to the com munity in which the Lodge exists.
In the area of the r itual, I can report a steady increase in the uniformity
of the work and the proficiency of the Inspectors in their ab ility to both
act and teach. There ap pears a minimum of the complaint "that's not
the way it was last year." Our s ystem of constant instruction continues
to show its bc1se of wisdom. and other jurisdictions query our methods
and emulate them.
Divisional coJ1ferenccs o f Inspec tors were held in accordance with
established practice. T he wor k of all degrees. including Lectures. by
Master and Candidate. was exemplified at eac h of the five conferences .
In Apr il. 1964, Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor, who had served
for fourteen yea rs as Assistant Gra nd Lecturer. Division IV, resig ned
that office and the G rand Master appointed Worshipful Wallace H .
Fiske. a Pas t Master of East Belt Lodge N o. 391, Tuolumne, and
Inspector of District No. 404, as his successor . Brother Fiske ably conducted the Fourth Division Conference and th e Ritual Committee welcomes him and wishes him every success. To Brother Taylor go all
our good wishes for a continued recu pera tion. The strong ties of fraternal rega rd and personal friendship have endeared Ray and his wonderful wife, Dora , to each of us w ho have known them over the yea rs.
