PROCEEOINGS OP THE

.

The Annual Lodge of Instruction for Inspectors, required by Section
I 56, 5th, was held October 10. 1964 at 25 Van Ness Avenue, San
Francisco, with Inspectors from each Division exemplifying the work.
The continuing high quality of the Inspectors' work promises well for
the Lodges.
The lnspectoral Corps is an important adjunct to the conduct of
Grand Lodge business throughout the year. The reliance of the Grand
Master for the execution of his aims and continuing programs of the
Grand Lodge lies most strongly on each Inspector. An Inspector who
is a leader, who commands the respect. loyalty and love of the Masons
of his District, can go far in aiding and assi·s ting the Grand Master.
More than this, he can be of inestimable strength to the Lodges and
the brethren.
In our labor of love for Masonry. the Grand Lecturer and the
Assistant Grand Lecturers have been long and consistent advocates of
strengthening the Inspectoral system . No legislation is necessary for
this. Dedication, devotion, leadership and love of the Fraternity are all
that are needed. Most of our Inspectors display these ornam'ents in
their every act.
At the lnspectoral level. we have placed the primary responsibility
for an adequate Candidate Coaching program. A mere recitation of
the catechism does not make either a knowledgeable or an enthusiastic
new Lodge member out of an applicant. Two years ago, by the vote of
this Grand Lodge. there became available to the Lodges, the "Handbook
for Candidates Coaches." The use of the handbook and the method of
certification of Coaches were entrusted in entirety to the Inspectors.
Individual reports made to me by the entire Inspectoral Corps indicate that the plan of broadened education for Candidates Coaches is
actively operating in over 90% of the Districts. We hope that the
remaining few will realize the interest that our membership has in its
own organization. Certainly, our so-called "ima ge," either "private" or
"public," will be better served if our membership has a greater knowledge of itself.
The Grand Lecturer has been privileged this year to make a trip to
the beautiful state of Hawaii. Not only did the Hawaiian Inspectors and
Officers Coaches perform, but the Candidates Coaches of the Lodges of
Oahu gave the Candidates Lectures. There is increasing skill in the
work. and the spirit of Masonry pervades the atmosphere of each Island.
At Lihue, Kauai. Kahalui, Maui, and at Hilo and Kailua, Kona on Hawaii,
we met with the members of the Lodges and their wives, continuing the
friendships made and making new ones. To each of them, a warm Aloha.
The privilege of serving with, and serving, our Grand Master has
made this a memorable year for me. His unassuming modesty and his
ability belie each other. The qualities of kindness and steadfast courage
show when the going is rough. I trust that he will remember his associ-

'th the Inspectoral Corps and the Ritual Committee as a satisfy.

Just prior. to the preparation of this report your Board suffered the

UNION CITY

In our report to you last year we asked tha t you cardully check your
applican ts for admission to the Homes before submitti n g their applications to the Board. We are again repeating this plea, with particular
reference to the physical qualifications of the applicants to our home in
Union City.
As you know, our entrance requirements require a ll a pplicants to be
in reasonably good health, able to take care of themselves and their
rooms and be completely ambulatory.
It has been most exasperating on many occasions during the past
year, after having a signed statement from a physician vouching for the
above qualifications. to find that the applicant ha s had to be h ospitalized
immedia tely upon arrival, oftentimes suffering from difficulties of long
standing, completely ignored in the doctor's report. We cannot understand this. b ut it explains our frequent request for an additional medical
report by a doctor of ottr designation if there is a nything in our files to
indicate its desirability. We further reques t tha t the original medical
report be made by an impartial examiner rather than a doctor friend of
the applicant or the lodge.
We repea t also that a more careful check on the part of the lodge
will often disclose the lack of qualifications of an applicant prior to having
the lodge request admission, with the attendant savings to the Board of
the expense of a social worker's investigation . Your careful compliance
with this request will be very much appreciated.
Please remember that if your problem is that of taking care of an
indigent aged brother, his wife or his widow, that admission to the Home
is not your only available help. If your applicant cannot physically qualify for admission to the H ome but qualifies in every other way. yo u may
apply for what we term "outside relief" and monthly assistance may be
granted to help you carry the load.
It should be borne in mind that the Masonic Homes of California is
a charity . The fact that a brother has had the privilege o f being a Mason
for a substantial number of years does not, in itself, automatically convey
to him the right to be our guest in his advancing years. We appeal to you
members of Grand Lodge, who are the leaders of our craft, to see to it
that this fact is more generally understood.

A recent survey of per capita costs of Home operation m t~e vano~s

REPORT OF THE SUPERINTENDENT COVINA HOME

Respectfully submitted,
GAIL H. DAVID, Superintendent

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is indeed a great pleasure to submit my sixteenth annual report as
Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina. for the
year ending June 30, 1964.
HoME MEMBERSHIP

As of June 30, 1964, the Covina Home shows approximately a
twenty-five percent increase over last year's population at the same time.
At present our Home Family numbers twenty-nine girls and thirty-nine
boys, for a total of sixty-eight children. Durin g the fiscal year of 19631964, twenty-four young people were admitted; thirteen boys and eleven
girls. Thus it will be seen that almost one-third of our present population
has been in the Home less than one year. Five boys and four girls were
above twelve years of age at the time of admission, which mea ns that
many of their living patterns were well-established prior to the moment
of entrance. Of the eleven youngsters who departed from the Home,
seven were boys, four were girls. Six of the children returned to live wi th
their families. The other five young people. who were graduated from
Charter Oak High School. will pursue the following program: one boy
will attend La Verne College; one boy California State Polytechnic College at Pomona; and the third young man has been accepted by the
United States Air Force. The two graduating girls will attend Ventura
Junior and U.C.L.A . college courses, respectively.

The children at Covina are, as usual, encouraged to participate in
many school and extracurricular activities. Placement of the Home
Family according to grade level is as follows: twenty-four children in
high school. seventeen in junior high, and twenty-seven in grade school.
Two graduates, Fred Clinkscale and Bruce Warrick, will live at the
Home while they attend La Verne College and California Polytechnic
College, respectively. They are, also, recipients of the H ome Scholarship
Fund.
A full and vigorous program for the continued develop ment of a
sound body and a healthy mind involves some of the following types of
activities: Athletics (school and H ome competition}; Swimming and
Lifesaving; Camping, Surfing, Boating, Fishing, water-skiing, horseback
riding; cultural visits, travel. Arts and Crafts; week-end trips; Museums
and Zoos. In addition, the children are encouraged to become members
of community you th groups such as Orders of Job's Daughters, D e

136

PROC EEDINGS OP THE

Molay, Rainbow for Girls. Campfire Girls. Brownies. Scouts. Little
League, and many other recognized and approved character and spiritual-building organizations. The Masonic Pioneers 4-H Club activities
also provide for growth and development for many of our family through
projects and shows where their efforts bring recognition and reward.
Supplementary tutoring help has been available for those children
who appeared to require it. both from the Home Teacher, responsible for
the usual academic subjects, and the specialized tutors who helped at
the high school level. Every effort is made to assist the youngsters to
achieve their potential. through remedial and accelerated tutoring programs. In addition to the above, a regular schedule of diagnostic testing
and counseling involving individual and group therapy is a part of our
planned program to meet each child's needs.
The staff of the Magan Clinic in Covina has continued to supervise
the medical and health program for the Covina Family, with the regular,
yearly examinations supplemented by additional consultations whenever
these are indicated. Ordinary dental care and hygiene are offered by a
visiting dentist at the Home hospital. Specialists supervise the care and
needs for problems connected with orthodontics. ophthamology. optom etry, orthopedics, plastic work, etc.
The contact between the Alumni and the Home is unique in the
history of Homes for children. The office maintains a roster of at least
five hundred current addresses. The yearly Newsletter devotes half its
pages to letters from graduates. Additionally, all of the Covina Home
Reunions are covered. A picnic in Sacramento on the first Saturday in
June, a Reunion at Covina on the second Sunday in September, and a
Dinner in San Francisco. the Saturday preceding Grand Lodge Communication, marked the year 1963. with the annual Dinner Dance taking
place in April of 1964. The San Francisco Dinner enjoyed the largest
attendance since its inception, with many of the diners traveling from
the Los Angeles area to be present. A number of the San Francisco
area Alumni came south for the dinner dance.
A sixteenth year is in a sense a kind of beginning again, for in some
respects the challenge of the Administration of the Home has been renewed by its increased population trend and the acceptance of older
children. The decrease in average length of Home membership affects
the continuation of some traditions. and, correspondingly, establishes
new ones.
As mentioned in my last report, I am. indeed. grateful for the opportunity to serve the children and the Fraternity. Many rich and rewarding
experiences are compensated to an individual privileged to serve children.
but especially is this true in our Home Family where the Fraternity
through the Board of Trustees is dedicated to the principle of Brotherly
Lov~.

Respectfully submitted
ROBERT M. HENRY, Superintendent

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board hereby submits its 32n<l
Annual Report. for your thoughtful consideration. covering the fiscal
year ending June 30, 1964.
PRINTED ITEMS Qp PUBLICITY

During the past year, the Lodges ordered 1.600.000 printed items of
publicity from the Endowment Board for sending to their members to
inform the brethren about our Masonic Homes. and to encourage them
to make a contribution to the Endowment Fund. The greater amount of
credit for this phase of our work goes to the Lodges. especially the
Lodge Secretaries, for the great amount of work involved in sending
such items to the members.
Something new was added a year ago and will be repeated this
coming season. Last year for the first time. this Board offered certain
"Christmas" and "Holiday" printed items for the Lodges to send to the
members in November and December. to encourage the brethren to
make a special "Christmas" or "Holiday Season" gift to the Homes
Endowment Fund. The Lodges ordered nearly 300.000 such items and
they met with such good success that additional ones are being offered
for the coming season.
BEQUESTS

Bequests in the amount of $106,661.77 were received into the
Endowment Fund from the Estates of brethren and their families and
friends who remembered the Homes Endowment in their Wills, and
thus left a Living Memorial to the Masonic Homes. This is in addition
to the bequests that were made directly to the Masonic Homes for new
buildings and other purposes.
The Endowment Board made an additional mailing of information
to the 1700 attorneys who are Masons whose names are on file with
the Endowment Board. In addition, the Lodges ordered 43,000 of our
pamphlets entitled "My Last Will and Testament" for mailing to
members.
INCO ME FROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND

The earnings from the Endowment Fund for the past year amounted
to $486.936.00 which amount was credited to the cost of maintaining
our Masonic Homes. The principal of the Endowment Fund always
remains intact. and only the income therefrom can be used in the operation of the Homes.

138

INDIVIDUAL PARTICIPATION

This past fiscal year, 118, l 96 individual brethren made contributions
to the Endowment Fund, for an increase of nearly 2,000 above a year
ago. These figures disclose that only 48 % of the brethren made a contribution to the Homes Endowment Fund. It is regrettable tha t the
load is carried by less than half of the members. We hope the Lodges
will "go all out" this coming year to materially increase the number of
contributors that "all may share" in this important phase of Masonry.
INDIVIDUAL CoNTRIBUTIONS THROUGH LooGES

Individual contributions this year amounted to $783,339.94 for an
increase of $42,098.47 above a year ago. This figure does not include
bequests, memorials, or special gifts from organizations. In addition, 52
Lodges sent in a total of $8.176.00 during the first 10 days o f July.
but which were received too late to be included in the audited figures as
of the close of the fiscal year on June 30th. Obviously, those late payments could not be included in the individual Lodge figures in subsequent p ages of this report, but will be included in the 1965 report.
272 Lodges decreased in amount of contributions this year.
The average contribution per member this year was $3 .20 as compared to $3.03 per member a year ago. The average per contributor
this year was $6.63 as compared to $6.37 the previous year. This
average "per contributor" figure seems to indicate that too many brethren are still thinking in terms of "$2 per member" which has long since
become obsolete.
This Board does not suggest any specified amount that each member
should give, and certainly not $2 per member which was started 30
years ago. Times have changed, and money values too. We think that
the amo unt of the contribution should be left to the individual brother
according to his finances, his conscience, and his concern for his fraternity and his less fortun ate brethren and their families.
H onor Roll status was attained by 637 Lodges this year, by averaging $2 or more per member. However, the $2 per member Honor Roll
is now considered as a mininmum - a mile-post or stepping-stone but not the real goal.
$3 OR M ORE AVERAGE P ER MEMBER
A much greater "Honor" than the Honor Roll is for a Lodge to be in
the special listing of those Lodg~ which averaged $3 or more per
member, listed as below according to average, a nd to be as high as

CHANGES IN ENDOWMENT BOARD PERSONAL

After serving on this Board for fifteen years, Byron Coleman asked
that he not be re-appointed to another term and he was replaced by
Haig Soghomonian. Past Master of Mission Lodge No. 169. Ralph
S. Brokaw asked not to be re-appointed, after seven years on the Board,
and he was replaced by C. Raymond Winterhalder, Past Master of
San Jose Lodge No. 10. For business reasons, Herschell E . Griffin
asked not to be re-appointed and was replaced by W. W. Reyburn,
Past Master of Garden Grove Lodge No. 586. To those who left the
Board, we say thanks so much for your long years of faithful service.
We know they will continue to enthusiastically support this great work.
OuR APPRECIATION To ALL
It is impossible to name and adequately thank all who have assisted
in this work of the Homes Endowment. All we can do is give a great
big all-inclusive thank you, first to M . W. Elmer W. Heald, Grand
Master, who expressed his concern and gave us a boost at every opportunity; to M. W. Edward H. Siemli, P .G.M ., Grand Secretary. Verne
W . Hendrix, Assistant Grand Secretary, and all members of the Grand
Secretary's staff for their willing helpfulness at every opportunity; to
Donald G. Campbell, Grand Lecturer, and his -staff of Assistant Grand
Lecturers and Inspectors who have assisted us so greatly; to the other
Grand Lodge officers and committeemen all of whom have given us moral
and material support; to the Masters, Secretaries and endowment committeemen of the Lodges, who have borne the lion's share of work
for the endowment Cause in the Lodges, and all other officers and members who have assisted them; to the Board of Trustees of the Homes,
and Robert M. Henry and Gail H . David and their wives, and the
members of the staff of both Homes, for all of these directly administer
to the daily needs and happiness of our children and elderlies; and last

144

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

but not least, to the 118.196 brethren who have shared of their means
that others less fortunate might have a good Home. All of the above
are a vital part of the Homes Endowment team and our thanks go to
every one of them.
IN CONCLUSION

And now, a new Masonic year dawns! Of greater opportunities for
service and devotion! Of greater needs and greater challenges!
A challenge to the officers and brethren of the 272 Lodges that
decreased in contributions this year, that they may re-double their
efforts for the coming year. A challenge . also, to the other 400 Lodges
which increased in contributions this year, that they may not experience
the disappointment of a decrease next year. The Endowment Board
accepts the challenge to "go all out" in our efforts to assist the Lodges
in attaining the greatest record for next year. To that end we offer our
time, our efforts. our experience and our printed material to all Lodges.
The appropriation of $17.000.00 which we hereby humbly request
will assist us in assisting you. Most of this amount will be spent for
printed material which we furnish to the Lodges.
We earnestly solicit the prayerful thoughts and devoted assistance of
every brother in the Jurisdiction, in order that we may adequately
endow our Masonic Homes for all time to come, and thus "insure the
continuance of loving care" to the less fortunate children and elderly
of our great Masonic family.
Respectfully submitted,
THE MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
JoHN M. GORDON. Chairman
KERMIT A. JACOBSON, Vice-Chairman (South)
KENT 0. SEYMOUR. Vice-Chairman (North)
PAUL A. PFLUEGER. Treasurer
EDWARD H. SIEMS. P .G .M .• Secretary

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F . & A. M. of California:
This is the Tenth Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the
California Masonic Memoria l Temple.
At the close of the 1963 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge the
Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple met in Annual Meeting. The President. Arthur M. Warren, reported the election of Theodore Meriam as Deputy Grand Master. Myron E. Smith as Senior Grand
Warden, and Laurence E. Dayton as Junior Grand Warden. On proper
motion they were duly elected members of the Board of Trustees as
provided in the California Masonic Code.
The Board then proceeded to organize with Arthur M. Warren.
Past Grand Master. as President. Ralph H. Head as Vice-President.
Paul A. Pflueger as Treasurer, and Edward H. Siems, Past Grand
Master and Grand Secretary. as Secretary.
The terms of the appointed members of the Board are as follows :
Expiring in 1964, Paul A. Pflueger and Samuel I. Jacobs, and expiring
in 1965, Lyle E. Patton and Ralph H. Head. and expiring in 1966, T .
Galt Atwood and Chester R. MacPhee.
It is the duty and responsibility of Trustees to report to its trustors
any loss or damage which occurs and which might impair the property or
the trust. So it is that the Trustees record an irreplaceable loss when on
May 21. 1964, its President, Arthur M . Warren. was summoned by the
Supreme Grand Architect. No finer monument can be erected to a man
than that which he himself built with his own hands inspired by his
heart and mind. This Memorial Temple, the Masonic Homes of California, and above all the Grand Lodge of California stand today on
firmer foundations because of the courage, the faith, and the endeavors
of Arthur Melvin Warren.
At a special Board Meeting on July 1O. 1964, Ralph H. Head and
Samuel I. Jacobs were called upon by the Trustees to serve for unexpired
terms as President and Vice-President.
Under the capable direction of George D. Gavin, serving his first
full year as building manager, rental income from the auditorium and
exhibit hall increased an exceptional 91 % while total rental increased
'11 %. Brother Gavin's years of activity in business and property development combined with his fraternal and community devotion have given
Memorial Temple an authoritative and enthusiastic entrepreneur. H is
report along with the complete audited financial statement of Lybrand
Ross Bros. & Montgomery are to be considered a part of this message.
The remaining debt of any significance on our financial statement is

MAINTENANCE

We have checked out all mechanical operations in the Temple a nd
a "built in" deficiency in our ventilating and hea ting system has been
corrected. Several economies have been made, which will have recurring
benefits to our operations.
We have completely adjusted our electrical usage to meet the de~
mands of the Temple. This has resulted in a reduction of electricity
usage sufficient to permit absorption of the increased costs, caused by
greater occupancy of the Temple and has made a net reduction for the
year of 7.7% .
Janitorial salaries, cost of supplies and services have been increase.cl
and this has been offset by economies in the purchase and use of supplies
and by our employees doing some of the work which was previously
contracted.
PAINTING

The exterior qf the Temple had not been painted for six years. A
large number of settlement cracks developed in the outer concrete walls.
This permitted water to seep in. The entire exterior, excluding the marble
areas, has been sealed and painted. It is not expected that this work will
have to be done again for at least eight years.
IN COME

Income from rentals, excluding the garage, has increased 91 % in
1964 over 1963, while operating expense increased 13% for the same
period (excluding the seal and the exterior pain t work the increase was

11/z o/o.)
GARAGE

Last year we reported a $9,000.00 increase in our garage revenue
participation. over the preceding year. We are pleased to report that the
twelve month period, July 1, 1963. to June 30, 1964, shows another sub~
stantial increase amounting to $7,150.00. The increased occupancy of the
Temple is, in part, responsible for this improvement. Each performance
in the Auditorium. or meeting in the Exhibit Hall. adds greatly to the
garage income.

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMISS ION
ON MASONIC PRACTIC ES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
With this report. the Special Commission on Masonic Practices
announces two largely unprecedent ed steps which it has taken. The
first is to return to the Treas urer unspent a substantial portion of the
funds budgeted to it for the past Masonic year. The second is its recommendatio n that its own existence be terminated.
The commission was created two years ago by the direct action of
Past Grand Master Ira Coburn. and was charged with the basic duty
of ascertaining from the membership of the Craft in California and
Hawaii what the problems of the Craft were as the membership saw
them, and what various suggestions might come from the Brethren as
to their solution. The commission was strictly a fact-finding body. As
such it interviewed great numbers of members. and gathered large quantities of material through the extensive use of questionnair es. All replies
to its inquiries were held in strictest confidence.
Thereafter, the commission made its firs t report which set out major
problem areas and suggested alternative solutions. The commission itself
made no recommenda tions as to action to be taken by the Lodges. but
earnestly requested each Lodge to analyze its own condition in light of
the report and then to experiment with such remedial suggestions as
might appeal to it. This procedure was strongly endorsed by the then
Grand Master.
During the past year, the commission has distributed over 30.000
copies of its report to the membership , has met with many Lodges and
District Officers' Association s to amplify and discuss its report. and has

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

at all times been available for consultation with any Lodge which wished
assistance in solving its own problems by resort to one or more of the
possible actions described in the report.

THE GEORGE WASHINGTON MASONIC
NATIONAL MEMORIAL

172

Thereafter, Grand Master Heald directed the Masters of all Lodges
to report on action, if any, taken by them as a result of the suggestions
made in the commission's printed report.
From the Masters' responses received up to July 1st, it appears that
various suggestions presented in the commission's report have received
substantial support and have been put in practice. Principally, these
suggestions include action in beginning and ending meetings on time.
with a carefully worked out order of business; definite programs to locate,
attract and bring sojourners into active Lodge participation; the impressing upon all members of the broad areas concerning which it is wholly
permissible and appropriate to talk about Masonry to non-members; real
activity to improve the physical appearance of Lodges both inside and
outside; a heavy increase in social activities bringing the whole families
of members into personal contact with Masonry and those active in it
and the highly successful formation and regular use of telephone committees to stimulate attendance at Lodge affairs.
The commission is gratified by these results of its study. and especially so because concrete results in increased attend;:mce, renewed member interest and improved public relations are already apparent.
There remain, however, problem areas of grave concern in respect
to which increasing effort must be made for the strength and health of
the Craft. These areas include, among others, the achievement of better
leadership for many of the Lodges. the development of more meaningful
education in the great spiritual truths which undergird the dignity and
purpose of the individual in relation to the universe, the proper support
of youth activities to combat the lowering of standards and an increased
activity of the Craft in meaningful public ceremonies and observances.
To abandon these areas is to this commission unthinkable. But each
of these areas is beyond the commission's charter, and falls within the
responsibility of the Grand Master and this Grand Lodge.
For this reason, your Commission on Masonic Practices believes that
its own special project has been completed and that the implementation
of the many advances yet to be made by the Fraternity in this Grand
jurisdiction should pass to those especially empowered so to do.
Respectfully submitted.
ROBERT B. WATTS

A. BARTLETT Moss

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
This is a report on The George Washington Masonic National
Memorial located on Shooters Hill at Alexandria, Virginia-the memorial erected to the memory and in honor of our first President, George
Washington, Master Mason.
Of all the memorials dedicated to one who was so aptly described as
"Father of our Country"-memorials in the form of monuments, paintings. sculptures, essays, poems, documents, etc.-the memorial erected
on Shooters Hill is the one of which we as Masons are most proud for
it was conceived in the minds of brethren who felt that one so illustrious
as George Washington should be memorialized in tangible form by the
Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons in which our distinguished
brother was an earnest and devoted member.
Briefly, my brethren, on February 22. 1910, the groundwork for our
Memorial was laid when representatives from 18 Grand Lodges met in
Alexandria-Washington Lodge No. 22 to consider proposals fo r a
memorial in the form of a monumental type building which would not
only be inspirational in design but would also provide adequate space
to house and safely preserve the Washington relics which were then
in the old Lodge room in downtown Alexandria. As planned, the memorial building was to provide space for several Lodge rooms, space for
other M asonic organizations , a library and a museum , and for galleries
in which to <lisplay paintings, sculptures and other forms of art of interest and importam:e to Masons . And all this was to be in a place rich
in landmarks, atmosphere and traditions of the Virginia countryside,
where our revered brother spent his entire lifetime except for the years
which he gave in service to his Country.
Our records indicate that our distinguished ·senior living Past Grand
Master, Oscar Lawler. was among those who gave their support to the
proposed memorial project.
The Memorial Association was permanentiy organized the following
year on February 22, 1911; ground for the Memorial was broken on June
5, 1922 and the cornerstone was laid on November l, 1923 under the
auspices of The Grand Lodge of V irginia in the presence of some 25,000
persons including President Calvin Coolidge, Chief Justice William H .
Taft and the Grand Masters of all Grand Jurisdictions in the Nation.
Eight and one-half years later, on May 12, 1932-the George Washington Bicentennial Year-the Memorial was dedicated at the largest
meeting of its kind ever held, with President Herbert Hoover assisting.
So, from an arduous beginning. followed by years of hard work and
lack of adequate fina ncing, the efforts begun by our brethren fifty -four
years ago to provide Masons and all Americans whithersoever dispersed

174

175

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

with a suitable a nd appropriate Masonic Memorial to our distinguis hed
brother have borne fruit.
A word about the physical aspects of the M emorial. Located on a
36 acre site, once considered as the site for our national capitol, the
memorial building. 168 feet wide. 248 feet long and 333 feet high on an
elevation of I 08 feet above sea-level. affords a beautiful. panoramic view
of the City of W ashington six miles distant. the City of Alexandria at
the foot of the hill and. to the north, historic Arlington- the final resting
place of so many illustrious in the history of our N ation. Then, to the
south , on the Potomac River, lies Mt. Vernon , the home and hallowed
shrine of him who we honor by this Memorial.
Contained within the building are rooms and exhibits rich in Masonic
lore and interes t.
Time will not permit a complete description of the interior-but of
prime interes t is The Replica Lodge Room with the furnishings used in
the Lodge over which George Washington presided as M as ter; the great
Memorial H all with its eight 60-ton polished green granite columns and
the two large 46 x 18 foot murals-one depicting the Laying of the Cornerstone of the United States Capitol. September 18, 1793 with President W ashington officiating at the Masonic ceremony ; and the other
showing General Washington attending a religious service on St. John's
Day. December 28. 1778 in Christ Church. Philadelphia. Pennsylvania.
These fine murals. my brethren, were presented to the Memorial by the
Grand Lodge of California on February 22, 1957. The central point of
interes t in the Memorial Hall is, of course, the heroic bronze statue
depicting Brother George Washington as M aster of his Lodge. The
statue is 17'3" high and weighs nearly eight tons.
There is so much more of interest which could be told but I will
confine any further description of the interior to the "Twelve Dioramas
of Events in W ashington's Life" which are on display in the Assembly
Room. These Dioramas. d epicting important events in the life of George
Washington. are mos t unique, beautiful and of great his torical interest.
We in California a re mos t interested in them for it was our own
Lloyd E. Wilson, Pas t Grand Master and Pas t Grand Secretary. who
conceived the idea of the Dioramas and actua lly s upervised the entire
work from the beginning until final installation. Lloyd Wilson's heart
and soul were in the Memorial. He served as a director of the Association from February 22, 1941 until his passing in Nove mber, 1961 and
he was a member of the E xecutive Committee for over 15 years of his
total service to the Association. Thus, the Diora mas become a memorial
to the memory of our beloved brother, Lloyd E. W ilson, as well as to
George Was hington . I was most honored when, on F ebruary 22 , I 962,
I was elected a Director of the Association for the unexpired portion of
Brother Wilson's term and again in 1963 when I was elected to serve a
three year term expiring F ebruary 22. I 966.

A final word relates to the financia l and operating aspects of the
Memorial.
Since the beginning of construction in 1922. a pproximately $7.500,000 has been spent for land. building. general expenses. maintenance and
operation of grounds and building. This figure does not include the value
of don a ted art and furnishings . the $50,000 pipe organ. the $25,000
Celesta-Chime Carillon and other valuable items.
Recent independent appraisals for insurance purposes indicate a
replacement cost of improvements at $14.320,000. an appreciable increase
over the actual cost of building and equipment (excluding grounds and
maintenance) of $5.243,000.
The Memorial Association has a goal of $5.000,000 for its Endowment Fund of which approximately $2.000,000 is at hand. In addition,
there is a Maintenance and Operations Fund which fluctuates from year
to year as contributions are received and improvements are made.
Each year, in conjunction with the Conference of Grand Masters of
North America, the annual meeting of The George Washington Masonic
National Memorial Association is held on February 22, unless it falls
on a Sunday, at the Memorial in Alexandria, Virginia. Active members
of the A ssociation are the Masonic Grand Lodges of the United States
and its possessions. Each member Grand Lodge has one ( 1) vote and is
represented by its Grand Master or his proxy. The annual business
meeting is conducted by the President of the A ssociation and. as a fitting
climax. contributions for the Endowment Fund and the Maintenance and
Operations Fund are received from the Grand M asters, or their proxies,
repres enting their. Grand Lodges and from other Masonic Bodies.
By provision in our law. all applicants for the degrees of Masonry
contribute $1.00 to the Endowment Fund of the George Washington
Memoria l and we are one of 42 Grand Lodges participating in this manner. Some Grand Lodges contribute to both Funds. It is gratifying to
know tha t over the years, California Masons have contributed $538.872
to the Memorial. and that we rank third among all Grand Lodges in
total contributions. In 1963, we stood sixth in contributions for the year.
However, other Grand Lodges which did not respond as liberally in
earlier years as did California are now coming to the fore and. naturally.
we a re mos t happy that such is the case. And to you Mas ters of Lodges.
please impress your candidates with the importa nce of the great Memorial and of what is symbolizes-and a lso of the importa nce of the very
small contribution we require of them in support of the Memorial.
The M emorial Association needs to realize its goal of a $5.000,000
Endowment Fund from which can be derived earnings sufficient to maintain the Memorial in top physical condition.
Its operation is directed by a devoted group of Masons. twenty- one
in number, serving as directors. Particularly do I commend the President.
M.W. John H. Hessey of Maryland for his capable and untiring efforts

176

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

and also those directors who serve on the Executive Committee. Truly,
theirs is a labor of Masonic love.
This is only a capsule report, so make it your business, my brethren,
to learn all you can about the Memorial. Visit it and urge the members of
your Lodges to do so when they are visiting on the E astern seaboard.
You will be well rewarded for your effort.
But keep in mind, the Memorial is not solely a pile of brick and
mortar. To understand the real meaning and purpose of the Memorial.
I quote the aim set forth by those who began this great undertaking so
many years ago. The quotation states, so beautifully, what the M emorial
means. It reads:
"We could not hope to increase the fame of Washington nor
add to the enduring luster of his name. Our purpose was, and is,
to hand down to coming generations a testament of the love of our
Fraternity for him who was the glory of his country and an ornament
to Freemasonry .... We could not fulfill our wishes by the creation
of a new planet to shed its splendor among the stars. We could not
set to music the ceaseless surgings of the sea to carry the message
of our appreciation to every shore throughout the coming years. So.
turning from the domain of the impossible, we opened the gra nite
hills of New Hampshire to take their strength and make it a ttest
our everlasting admiration for him to whom it is dedicated. Erected of
enduring materials, our temple will stand throughout the ages. It
will carry to generations yet unborn, and to those to whom we ma y
seem an ancient race, the message of human brotherhood. It will
perpetuate the attributes of self-denial. patriotism, love of country
and fellow man, which were typified in the life and work of the
great Mason, the master-build e r of our Nation - George
Washington."
Thus, my brethren, do we honor a great American, patriot, Statesman, Mason-a ma n who helped create the greatest memorial which we
possess-The Constitution of the United States of America. I believe
that if he could appear in this assembly today, he would reaffirm his
belief in the Constitution and challenge us to do the same.
Respectfully submitted,
GUY B. M1zE, Director

EMPLOY MENT BUREAUS

Brethren , their widows and orphans in securing employm ent. thereby

relief. The increasin g competit ion of our public placemen t agencies in
this field. as well as other factors, has occasion ed a decline in our placemen ts in the past year. and a correspo nding rise in the cost of each
placemen t. The Board of Control has been keeping a concerne d and
watchful eye on this trend for a number of years with the fear that if
it continue d, there might somewhe re come a time when the results in this
field might not justify their cost. The following figures briefly cover the

The records of the Grand Secretary's office reflect that many of the
Lodges are not shown as having adopted and submitted for approval a
copy of the Uniform Code o f By-Laws. T his was pointe~ ~ ut !n the
1963 report of this Committee. We urge that these defic1enc1es ~e
remedied by prompt action on the part of those involved. Toward this
end . correspondence is being continued with the individual Lodges , a.nd
we take this means of expressing our appreciation to those Lodges whic h
have com pleted the requested remedial a ction. This program will be
continued in the interest of the advantages which will result to the
Lodges themselves and to the supplying of complete records in the files
of the Grand Secretary's office.

advantage of having on file a consolidated record of the several details
of Stated Meeting dates. fees , dues and emergency relief provisions
under which they are currently operating.

is following an effective routine of promptly reviewing each item of

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON COMMERCI ALISM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
For the past few years this report has commenced substa ntially as
follows: "Your Committee on Commercialism is most pleased to report
that infractions of our laws, rules. and regulations continue to lessen in
scope, seriousness and number."
This report reflects no change from recent years. True there have
been some instances, where because of possible lack of direction by
responsible officers or thru inadvertence infractions have occurred. In
only one instance this year was a constituent Lodge involved; the principal offenders being appendant organizations having female members.
The excuse most frequently given being "lack of knowledge" from
which it is deduced that where a change in officers occurs. the outgoing
fail to pass on to the incoming, our regulations.
The Concordant OrganiZiltions have been most cooperative in seeking advice and clearance in regard to projects which they have had in
mind.
As to appendant groups we have found the severa l Shrine Temples
in the jurisdiction generally anxious to cooperate. A number of them
have met with us on occasion to discuss their ideas and problems, which
have to a large extent been worked out with reasonable satisfaction.
The football games and the other sporting events continue to be operated
within our regulations. and the certified audits which are received indicate costs within reason and a good return to the hospitals.
Last year's report mentioned a cemetery which had in its name the
word "Masonic" and which gradually thru the passing years had lost
its fraternal characteristics and was open to non-Masons. At its annual
meeting earlier this year this "Maso~ic Cemetery Association" voted to
change its name to "Acacia Memorial Park Association." There is another such "Masonic" cemetery now under our investigation, having
been given to this Committee only recently.
Because there had been no instances reporting activities of so-called
"Masonic" magazines published in this jurisdiction your committee
assumed that this problem was under control. but no such luck, a few
weeks ago we were jolted out of our complacency when our attention
was brought to the story of a newly obligated Entered Apprentice who
paid $300.00 to a salesman for an ad in one such publication. Upon
reflection this brother spoke to another brother who "set him straight"
and recommended that payment of the check be stopped. It was found
that the check had been cashed at once. We are now endeavoring to
develop further information to see if there is any avenue open thru
which we may be able to help this brother recover his money.
We have been involved in matters regarding so-called "Masonic"

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

187

publications originating in other Grand Jurisdictions. One such publication. the "Masonic Directory." privately owned in the mid-West, carries
lists of Grand Lodge officers and lis ts of concordant and appendant
groups together with pictures of many of these persons. The same long
distance phone and high pressure tactics selling advertising that we are
familiar with are used. This activity was called to the attention of the
Grand Jurisdiction in which the publication originates. In reply we were
advised "The Directory is not recognized nor authorized . . . but has
been tolerated for several years. Their method of solicitation is very
crude and high pressure selling by phone only"; a nasty condition
requires drastic action and not toleration.
Another such publication from the Northwest had a representative
in this state who was phoning banks in the State of Kansas using h igh
pressure and misrepresentin g the ownership. We received a com pla int
from the Grand Lodge of Kansas. A member of this Committee living
in the vicinity of this representative took this matter in hand and in his
investigation learned that the representative had suddenly moved to
another state.
An old and well known magazine specializing in mechanical matters
recently carried an ad reading "Masons (in very heavy lettering) send
today for a free catalogue of Masonic and Eastern Star books and
rituals." Upon communicating with the Grand Jurisdiction in which the
advertiser was located the Grand Master, in his reply, thanked us for
having brought the ad to his attention stating that he would take whatever corrective measures necessary.
A nationally published financia l newspaper carried an ad from a
person in New England offering a "3 inch Tubal Cane (two words
separated) for your car trunk or numberplate." This ad was called to
the attention of the Grand Lodge having jurisdiction in the area with
the request that the individual be contacted and asked to cease and
desist from such advertising in this Grand Jurisdiction.
In another instance the owner of a golf putting stand in Southern
California received a wire asking him to phone collect a party in Chicago
in regard to his putting stand. The person to whom he spoke stated he
represented the Masonic order and "wanted him to advertise in its
national magazine going to all Masonic Lodges throughout the country'':
cost of ad. $135.00. The stand own er claims no authorization was given ,
but he nevertheless became involved and was seeking our help and
counsel. Obviously under the circumstances there was very little we
could say or do.
For the past few years we have had problems with two so-called
"Masonic" periodicals. The Masonic Review Digest who used a Vancouver, B. C. address and The Freemason published in Oregon. We
recently were informed that the Post Office Department issued a fraud
order against these two publications which prevents any mail, including

During the past year securities were sold at prices yielding $1.235,052.29 more than their cost. thereby increasing the total asset value.
Since the inauguration of the Prudent M an Rule in 1950. this total
amounts to $4,402,865.90. Sales always rema in a part of capital assets,
and are never included in income total. With respect to the Endowment
Fund, no capital assets are ever withdrawn from this Fund.
Endowment Fund contributions made through Lodges amounted
to $783,339.94, for the year ended June 30, 1964. Other gifts and ·be~

quests for the Masonic Homes amounted to $473.976.45 (which also includes items other than stocks and bonds). The Masonic Homes Board
of Trus tees determines how these gifts and bequests are allocated-these
allocations are made in accordance with specific bequests, or in the absence of such , at the direction of the Trustees. The Endowment Fund
contributions remain in that Fund, and only the income is used.
The Charles Albert Adams H all situated at Union City ( Decoto),
which was referred to in the 1963 Investment Committee report, is nearing completion. This Hall is to house 91 additional residents. While the
total cost was estimated at $1.500.000, the amount of $939,023.52 was
withdrawn during the current year from the Masonic Homes of California General Fund, in addition to $354,000 which was withdrawn
during the previous year from the same fund, for the employees' dormitories at Union City.
May we also call attention to the fact that the total portfolio has increased since November, 1950. from $6.124 ,471 to $20,714,026, or about
238.22 9'c. and at the same time the income has increased from $120.598
to $738.717, or 512.54~c. As mentioned above. $1 .215.000 was withdrawn for the new Oecoto hospital in the year ending June 30, 1960:
$128,000 was withdrawn in the year ending June 30, 1962. to fund the
unpaid balance of the Grand Lodge Pension Fund: the amount of $354 .000 was withdrawn for the new dormitory a nd livi ng quarters for employees in the year ending June 30, 1963; a nd $939,023.52 was withdrawn in the current year ending June 30. 1964 for work on the Charles
Albert Adams Hall.

The Investment Committee would greatly appreciate your consideration of this request. Just write to the Grand Secretary for further informa tion.
The Investment C ommittee thought that a case history of one transaction which was practically closed during the current year might be of
interest. In 1949 the Masonic Homes of California inherited among
other items from the estate of James McCandless, of Honolulu, a few

195

shares of Pioneer Properties, whose sole asset was a block of the capital
stock of R iver Farms Company of California. At that time we were
offered $7.500 for these Pioneer Properties shares, which was not accepted.
In 1951 Pioneer Properties was liquidated in kind, without income
taxes, and the Masonic Homes of Ca lifornia received 1629 shares of the
capita l stock of River Farms Company of California. At that time $30
per share was the prevailing price of River F arms stock. During the
year 1963, River Farms Compa ny's propertie~, situated in Yol.o an.cl
Colusa C ounties. were sold. and the Masonic H omes of Cahforma
General Fund received $218.90 per share, or a total of $356,588.10. During the years that we owned the R iver Farms shares, dividends totalling
$68,825.25 were also received. making a grand total of $424,413.35.
There will probably be a tag end of approximately $3,000 more to
come, when the corporation is fin ally completely liquidated.
The entire portfolio is listed in the Grand Treasurer's a nd Auditors'
Reports, and therefore is not included herein. The securities are held in
safekeeping for account of Grand Lodge by the Trust Dpartment of the
Crocker Citizens National Bank, at its One M ontgomery Street Office,
San Francicso.
We have had excellent attendance at our Investment Committee
meetings during this year, as has b een the case since this Committee was
organized.
Again we come to tha t portion of the Investment Committee report
when we try to s ummarize in fe w words the financial a nd investment outlook as we see it.
We are presently pursuing a more conservative course. as already
indicated by the figures. with the objective of obtaining the greatest
amount of protection for our funds, under conditions as they exist.
As we said last year, the problems do not diminish , but we are prepared to meet them as they arise . Fortunately, we can move swiftly.
which we have done when necessary.
W e again repeat that our course of action can be quite different from
that of the individual for a variety of rea sons. This sta tement is made so
as not to influence personal actions.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary and his staff. a nd my thanks to
the members of the Investment C ommittee for their wholehearted and
generous cooperation at all times.
Respectfully s ubmitted on behalf of the Inves tment Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
LODGE FINANCING

The committee again calls to your attention the importance of main taining the temples in proper order and repair. The brethren must
realize that they have an obligation not only to themselves and all of
those who use the facilities of their temples. but also a definite obligation
to the community to keep them in a well-ordered manner thereby con~
tinuing pace with the growth of the community in which they are a
part. So much can be done with Yery little financing and effort. We urge
you to return to your temples and view them inside and out with ~ritic~l
eyes with the purpose in mind of keeping them and the surroundings JI\
such condition that they will retain the respect and support of the community, which is so necessary and important for the growth and dignity
of our fraternity.
The committee further recommends that continued study be made of
the financial condition of the lodges relating to insurance and tax requirements. It is most important that the temples be properly insured in
order that all who have the benefit of its use may be protected from loss
by liability. fire. theft and other matters normally covered by sufficient
and proper protection. Also. the requirements to mainta'.n a tax exem_pt
status must be strictly adhered to in order to comply with the essential
requisites of state and federal tax laws so that no critici~m may. be
pointed to any lodge or temple association or the fra ternity allegmg
that they are disregarding the requirements of the law. We. as Masons.
who so strongly promote the American way of life must set an example
of this belief by conforming to the laws of the land.
The past year's activities of the committee are included in detail
in the following pages of this report and will be published in the

The success of the past year has been due mostly to the coo peration
secured from the officers a nd brethren of the lodges and temple associations. It is our specinl desire to acknowledge our apprecia tion for the
complete and full support. counsel and advice given by our Gra~d Master. Elmer W. Heald . and his officers. Their assistance aided us m many
troublesome situations and has encouraged us in all our endeavors. Our
gratitude is also expressed to the Grand Secretary. the Assistant G.ra.nd
Secretary and to their efficient and accommodating staff for prov1dmg
us with needed ·a ssistance and cooperation. Such assistance and such
cooperation has made our task a much lighter one and our service on the
committee very rewarding .
Masonry is growing in strength in California and will continue to
grow as long as the interest in building new temples and improving those
in existence endures. We challenge the statement that we are no longer
operative but speculative only . Masons are builders-builders of temples where they may meet on common ground to mold the minds of men
to become better Masons and citizens and where they may dwell together
in peace and unity and harmony as free men under the benignant a nd
approving eye of the Great Architect of the universe .
Respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
As reported at the 1963 Annual Communica tion, your Committee on
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges has had under consider<1tion requests from two of the State Grand Lodges of the Republic of Brazil for
recognition by the Grand Lodge of California : First , the Grand Lodge
of Pa rana, founded in 1941. and , second , the Grand Lodge of Mat·.)
Grosso, organized in 1962.
Our information on these two Grand Lodges is tha t they form a p<ut
of the State Grand Lodge system of Brazil. that they a re entirely regular
and worthy of recognition. We, therefore, recommend that the Grand
Lodge of California extend fraternal recognition to the Grand Lodge
of P a rana, Brazil, and to the Grand Lodge of M ato Grosso. Brazil.
A s information. we report that the Grand Lodge formerly known as
the Grand Lodge of Rio de Janeiro in the fo rmer F ederal D istrict of the
City of Rio de Janeiro has now changed its name to the Grand Lodge
o f the State of Guanabara. This change was brought about by removal
of the Capital o f Brazil from Rio de Janeiro to Brasilia. The territory
for merly incorpora ted in the Fede ral District. incl uding the City o f Rio
de Janeiro, has now become a State known as Guanabara.
Respectfully submitted,
PHIL N . MYERS
ALFRED F. B RESLAUER
WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, JR.

Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Constitution O bservance is pleased to repor t to
this Annual Communication that during the past Masonic year there
was a steady and continuing progressive trend in the results of this program throughout the jurisdiction; the Master's reports to this Committee
have been carefully analyzed , and these reports from the Lodges indicate
to us first, that a ttendance at their local celebrations has, on a n average
throughout the jurisdiction . increased by approximately twenty per cent
( 20 % ) due to outstanding efforts in certain areas, and secondly. that .
in the opinion of our Masters. the approach used this year. and most of
th e programs presented by the Lodges have resulted in a decided improvement; and obviously attendance and effectiveness of programming
at these events are the most reliable and valuable cri teria in determining
the ex tent of enthusiasm and interest for this most worthwhile program
of your Grand Lodge. At this point, it should be pointed out that the

work of this Committee has been expanded. and a dditional patriotic
programs, other than Constitution Observances. have been promoted
throughout the jurisdiction in a very effective manner; this expansion
was in accordance with the policy adopted at the 1963 Communications
of our Grand Lodge, stating tha t " the work of the Constitution Observa nce Committee be expanded, with more programs and a dded activity."
(Pa ge 283, 1962 Proceedings.}
Our Grand M aster, the Most W orshipful Elmer W . Heald, has sincerely and effectively supported ou r program with dedication and enthusiasm throu ghout the year; you r Committee wishes to acknowledge that
muc h credit is r igh tfully due to our Gra nd Master for the progress
reported here. The Constitu tion of the U nited S ta tes. the " Let Freedom
Ring" Program and the various local " Flag D ay" Progra ms have found
their way into the subj ect matter of many of his inspirational addresses
to the Craft. during the year; also. your Gra nd Master has wholeheartedly supported the new mass media communication program, repor ted
later herein. and for his dedicated concern and effective support for our
entire program, ea ch member o f the Committee expresses sincere appreciation and gratitude. W e sincerely feel that our Grand M aster is one
of our great living Americans.
The added interest shown in the 1964 progrnm throughout the jurisdic tion is, no doubt, due to many fac tors and activities. The yea r itself.
being an election year, has focu sed added attention, to some degree,
to our Constitut ion Program; however, this factor has also restricted
agg ressiveness somewhat in this program fo r the year. since politics and
the expression of. political opinion at our celebrations cert ainly have no
place in this Masonically sponsored program. and a few of our Lodges
have expressed concern over this very problem.
Your Committee also reports that the Lodges procured an d distr ibuted an additional 80.000 "Preamble" promotional pieces dur ing the
year, or a total of 210.000, and our Master's Reports clearly indicate a
very close relationship between the use of these promotional pieces and
their total attendance at the celebrations.
From the Master's Reports, it is indicated that ninety per cent
( 90 % ) of the celebrations this year were public observances; your Committee feels that this is a healthy trend. w hereby the Masonic image.
and one of the tenets of the Craft, are being favorably projected into the
public at large. As a n indica tion of this trend, we are proud to report
t hat the Brethren in our sister State of H awaii he ld a highly successful.
yet dignified and well organized. public obser vance at which there were
in a ttendance approxima tely 4000 Americans.
This year, your Committee also embarked on a new program of promoting this Grand Lodge P rogram throu gh the mass media of radio and
television. At a very modest expense to your Grand Lodge, ever y television and rad io station in the State of California was fo rwarded "pub-

lie service" announcements for use by their stations, either copy to be
used by their local personalities or recordings and television slides for
their use. Your Committee contacted radio and television stations in the
State of California, together with letters from your Committee and the
public relations firm assisting us in this project. urging these stations to
use our material, and assuring them that this was a non-political and
non-controversial project of this fraternity. With reference to this particular activity, much ground work has been done in the field, which we
hope will be expanded in the future. Also your Lodges report that radio
and television coverage appeared in approximately forty-five per cent
( 45 % ) o( the areas. However, this activity is actually in its infancy, and
we hope it will be expanded markedly in the next year; your Committee
believes that this approach to the public could really be the vehicle
whereby our Constitution would again become a part of our daily lives;
actually. the possibilities of this approach are spectacular. Certain members o( our Fraternity are entitled to special recognition in this report
for their efforts and wholehearted cooperation to this new program, and
we refer specifically to Brother William Latta, of the Latta Co .• a public

Francisco, California; in this initial entrance into this field, these Brethren. who are professionals in this very specialized field. have given us
complete cooperation, and have rendered service to our Craft far beyond
the call of duty.
Your Committee wishes to express its appreciation and gratitude to
the personnel of the Grand Secretary's office, who have been most cooperative, and also the Inspectors throughout the jurisdiction are to be
congratulated for their cordial support and enthusiasm shown on behalf
of this program.
Finally, we recognize that the responsibility for success of this program rests with the Masters and Wardens of our Constituent Lodges.
and we are happy to report that our Masters and Wardens have accepted
this responsibility in a creditable manner.
In conclusion, your Committee makes the following recommendations
to this Grand Lodge:
1. Your Committee renews the recommendation of the 1963 Committee on Constitution Observance that this Committee be made a Standing Committee of this Grand Lodge, since the activities of this Committee deal with one of the most important and worthwhile programs of the
Craft.
2. That the budget for the 1965 Committee on Constitution Observ-

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Cemeteries submits the following report of its
accomplishments and activities during the Grand Lodge Year.
Our efforts during the past year have, for the most part, been most
gratifying. We have. however, had our share of disappointments.
FIDDLETOWN: Most of the improvement activity of this Committee during the past year has been centered around the Grand Lodge
owned cemetery at Fiddletown. This cemetery is located in the Mother
Lode Country about six miles east of Plymouth. The portion with which
we are concerned consists of approximately two acres in the shape of an
"L." extending 386 feet from the road to the back fence line and 208
(eet across the back. The balance of the cemetery is owned or controlled
by other fraternal and church organizations, and to the community.
This cemetery. as reported in the past , was in a deplorable condition.
being covered with weeds, brush, broken trees, broken fences, broken
headstones and curbs. and in general was a disgrace to the Fraternity.
We are pleased to report that it is now enclosed with an attractive chain
link fence with galvanized posts and corners. The entire area has been
cleared of alt weeds, brush, and unwanted trees. and the stumps treated

During a routine inspecti on of cemeteries in the Mother Lode C ountry, a most interest ing and pleasan t discove ry was made. We were
accomp anied on a portion of the trip by Brother Leslie E . Woodw orth.
a member of M adison Lodge No. 23 . Several years ago Brother Woodworth and a friend. who is a member of the Odd Fellows , came upon
the old Red Dog Cemete ry in a backwo ods portion of Nevada County
.
At that time. only one headsto ne was visible because of the grow th of
brush and trees 'and the accumu lation of rubbish over the years.
two men took upon themsel ves the task of cleaning up the a rea and
found that there existed two identica l sections in the middle of the
cemeter y about 40 feet square and complet ely enclosed by broken- down
metal fences. One section is marked with the Odd Fellows emblem on
the gate and the other with the M asonic level over the gate archwa
y.
This was the cemeter y of Mount Carmel Lodge No. 155 in Red Dog
which surrend ered its charter on August 16, 1872. There are approxi
mately 20 Masonic graves in this section.
Brother Woodw orth and his friend. Mr. Lyle White. have completely cleared off a ll the brush . weeds and debris, reset and pieced
togethe r the old headsto nes and restored the fence a s much as they
possibly could. The cemeter y is now in excellen t conditio n and would
be a credit to any Lodge. A visitors ' register has been kept since 1958
and approxi mately 1000 people, from all over the world. sig n the book

each year.
Brother Woodw orth and Mr . White a re to be commen ded for a
tremend ous job exceptio nally well done. It is recomm ended by this Committee tha t a further study be made of the Red Dog C emetery and report
made to Grand Lodge at the next session.

Brother Woodworth has also located. and restored in equally ftne
condition, three Masonic graves in the old Omega Cemetery. Three
identical stones mark these graves of brethren who were evidently members of Dibble Lodge No. 109 in Omega, which surrendered its charter
on September .27, 1879. We feel that a similar study should be made
of this cemetery and a report made at the next session.
Our congratulations must go to Chico Lodge No. 111 and Brother
Wilton L. Simmons for an excellent job of restoring the old M asonic
section of the Chico Cemetery. This particular section was donated to
the lodge in the early 1850s by General John Bidwell. Maintenance of
the area was not placed directly upon Chico Lodge but within the past
year members made it a project of their own. Volunteer work groups
meet on Sunday to clear out trees and shrubbery, which practically covered the area. They have been assisted in their project by members of
Chico Assembly, Order of Rainbow for Girls. who have worked raking
the entire section. We feel that all other Lodges that own cemeteries
should take a lesson from Smartsville and Chico and do the same thing.
A request was made of our Grand Master, by " Memorial Park
Cemetery" at Brea, for a ruling as to whether or not an altar with an
open Bible could be placed in the Acacia Lawn section, and if the Grand
Lodge would perform the Masonic Dedication Ceremonies. It was the
opinion of Most Worshipful Elmer W . Heald that an altar with the
open Bible could be placed in the Acacia section but with no inscription
taken from our ritual. or manual or any other inscription of strictly
Masonic nature. It was also his opinion that a Grand Lodge dedication
could not be made because the section was privately owned. and was not
strictly a Masonic Section.
To continue with the work already being done, we respectfully

Kentucky, Georgia. Oklahoma and Illinois are some of ·the· jurisdictjons
which have such publicntions. Two years ago T exas joined this group.
At that time the Grand Master of that State informed his Grand Lodge
that aside from the desirability of providing each member with a Masonic
publication the importance of maintaini ng a central mailing list of members is an absolute necessity for the future opera tion of Grand Lodge.
The new Texas magazine is an outstanding example of Maso nic journalism. It has adopted some of the policies we have endeavored to follow.
Thus it has declared: " For the most part, we must leave the learned
treatises to the scholars and the Research Lodges. We must not over-do
the material on ritual. We must carefully weigh material of interest
only to Lodge Officers. We must avoid that which is interesting to one
section of the State but of no real interest in oth er sections. W e must try
to appeal to those who attend Lodge but never try to appeal only to
those who do."
The avowed purposes of the Texas Magazine a re very similar to our
own. Paraphrasing the statement of purpose we say: The sole purpose
of California Freemason is to strengthen, support and serve Blue Masonry. It has no other purpose.
In serving this purpose. California Freemason is dedicated to: {I )
keeping Masons, their families and friends inform ed on Masonic activities, issues and programs; ( 2) promoting and cultivating Masonic
thinking, acting and living; (3) encouraging Masons to improve themselves as individuals and as a community of men, bound together by
the fraternal ties of Brotherhood under the Fatherhood of God: ( 4)
inspiring all Masons to increased civic endeavor and better citizenship.
that the world at large may be a better place for all mankind to live.
At the request of the Grand Master we obtained firm bids for the
preparation and mailing the magazine of the same format as used during
the past year to all members of the California Lodges. The unit cost
decreases as the quantity increases. We have a firm bid to print the
four issues for a total of .196c per subscription. Mailing bids provide for
mailing at a unit price of .029c and postage would amount to .022c.
This would make a total unit price of 24.7 cents per subscription.
The number of Lodges which send the magazine to their entire membership has gradually increased. This year the Grand Master set the
contribution to be remitted by these Lodges at 50 cents per member as
shown on the official return for the previous year.

REPORT OF BOARD OF
LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Board of Library Commissioners herewith submits its report
for the year 1963-64.
LIBRARY ACQUISITIONS
The Library acquired by gift this year 161 volumes and by purchase.
at a cost of $200.36. 42 other volumes. Chiefly. the purchased volumes
are for general circulation among the brethren ; only one is a long-needed
reference book.
Among books acquired by gift were:
.
Sacred Books and Early Literature of the East, 13 volumes. gift of
Brother Charles C. Goodale.
Proceedings of the M idwest Conference on Masonic Education . 8
volumes, gift of Iowa Masonic Library.
Several histories of lodges, published in connection with their centennial celebrations. gifts of the lodges concerned.
.
Several books dealing with Hawaii and one rare and valuable Brief
History of the Scottish Rite. acquired from the library of the late Grand
Master Atkinson.
ACCESSION OF BOOKS
Accession of all volumes in the Library was completed, insofar as
the accession list of any growing library can ever be completed . and
shows we closed the year with a total of 2,349 books and pamphlets.
This list of books is of special value for insurance purposes; in event of
any loss by fire or otherwise it will enable us to make an exact claim for
compensation.
MusEUM AcQUISITIONS
The Library also gained a number of valuable Museum items. Amo ng
these were the ballot box. original minute book. one gavel and one apron
used by the extinct Bodie Lodge No. 252 which was located in the
(now) ghost town of Bodie.
. .
Two very handsome silver trowels used by Grand Master Wilham
W. Traylor in laying the cornerstones of the courthouses of Stockton
and Los Angeles. in 1879.
.
A 33rd degree jewel once belonging to Dr. J. D. Kergan . of Detroit,
the gift of Mrs. Josephine Kergan.
THE ADAMS PAPERS
We were also the recipients of the Masonic papers of the late Past
Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, comprising 151 items dealing
with Mexican Masonry. Negro Masonry, Public Schools Week- which
it will be remembered he founded- and some general addresses made
by him on Masonic subjects.
These papers are being placed in a special file as THE ADAMS CoL-

MODEL OF SOLOMON'S TEMPLE

Last year Brother Edward A. Hudson. of Paso Robles, offered Grand
Lodge a model of King Solomon's Temple upon which he had expended
some 5,000 hours of time and a considerable sum of money. Your Commission recommended acceptance of this offer and the appropriation of
sufficient money to provide a case in which the model might be displayed.
Grand Lodge saw fit to reject this recommendation because. we
believe, the Brethren were not satisfied that the model was (a) authentic
and ( b) of such workmanship and general excellence as to be compatible
with the beauty and dignity of our magnificent Memorial Temple.
Brother Hudson informed us several months ago that this offer was
still open, that there were no conditions whatever attached to it and
that he would welcome inspection of the model that we might see for
ourselves what he was offering. Accordingly. several Grand Lodge
officers and committeemen made special stops in Paso Robles to inspect
it. They uniformly received such a favorable impression and were so
enthusiastic about the project that your Commission is impelled to
renew its recommendation this year.
Following are some special points to be considered:
1. There are of ·c ourse a number of models of King Solomon's
Temple in existence. based on at least three different interpretations of
the Biblical references.
2. This model is based upon the interpretation of facts given in
First Kings and Second Chronicles by Dr. John Wesley Kelchner, an
archreologist and Biblical scholar. Dr. Kelchner spent many years and
a fortune in money in the study of this great edifice.
3. Dr. Kelchner took his data to the noted architect Harvey Wiley
Corbett, under whose direction they were transformed into a series of
drawing·s, plans and skillful architectural renderings.
4. These drawings and plans were what Brother Hudson followed
in constructing his model. They were also followed in the construction
of the smaller and less elaborate model of the Temple which is now on
display in the Masonic pavilion at the World's Fair in New York.
5. Corbett stated that these drawings, prepared under his supervision, reproduce "exactly the spectacle beheld by the eyes of Solomon
when his workmen had finished." Your Commission is not qualified to
vouch for the accuracy of this statement but we are satisfied that these
plans, and Brother Hudson's model, are as nearly authentic as it is
possible for human genius to achieve at thi·s modern date.
6. As a further assurance of authenticity Brother Hudson, before
beginning construction of this model, visited both Egypt and the Holy
Land to satisfy himself that there were available, at the time of the

ABOUT THE MODEL ITSELF

Brother Hudson's model is no small creation. Built accurately to
scale, it stands 39 inches high, is 37 inches wide and 69 inches long.
In it the details of the Temple are reproduced minutely. The ground
floor of the Temple. the win ding stair, the pillars of the porch and
everything else of Masonic significance are all there. One side of the
model is open, in part, revea ling the Middle Chamber, the H oly of
Holies, the Ark of the Covenant and other items which the Bible says
were within the Temple. Concea led electric lights can be switched on
by viewers to illuminate these.
Your Commission sincerely believes that this model is worthy of our
acceptance and display and that, in the words of one Grand Lodge
officer. "it will direct a lot of favorable attention toward Masonry."
PROTECTING THE MODEL

Naturally. so intricate and valuable a model must be protected from
dust, vermin and souvenir hunters, of whom there are undoubtedly a
number among the many thousands of persons who attend non-Masonic
functions in the Memorial Temple every year, to say nothing of casual
visitors. Your Commission therefore recommends that an appropriation
be made for a suitable case to shelter and protect the model.
Five manuf~cturers were asked whether they cared to bid on ~;uch
a case. One declared itself unable to meet our requirements; three failed
to answer our invitation to bid and only one, the Library Bureau of
Remington Rand, submitted a bid. This is the same organization which
has supplied us with the two cases now in use on the second floor of
this temple and the proposed case would be of similar construction and
compatible design.
Owing to the pressure of time, this Remington Rand bid was fig ured
locally and was offered us as an "outside figure" with verbal assurance
that after study by the bidder's engineering staff in Herlimer, New Yor k,
a substantial reduction might be expected. To be on the safe side, however, your Commission is using in this report the bid as made, $3,344. 12,
with the assurance to Grand Lodge that no more of this amount will be
expended than is necessary.
It should be borne in mind that this is a very large case-nearly 80
inches long , 41 inches deep and 45 inches high. with a base 32 inches
high. In view of prices paid for previous cases, and of the rise in costs
of materials and labor, your Commission feels that the price asked is
reasonable.
