PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This tabulation shows the Lodges and the number of Sojourner affiliations made by each, up to four. The Lodges with from one to three
affiliations each are not listed separately to conserve space. There are
304 Lodges in this category with a total of 454 Sojourner affiliations.
or over half of our total gains. This indicates how little things can count
up and that a few affiliations by the many will more than outweigh larger
numbers by a few. It is the work of the many that counts.
The following Lodges, which were given honorable mention in the
1963 Report by my esteemed predecessor. Brother Cohendet. equaled
or excelled their 1963 Sojourner affiliations: Home No. 721-9; Arcadia
No. 547-8; Lemon Grove No. 736-8; Table Mountvin No. 124---6;
Palo Alto No. 346-6; Palm Springs No. 693-6; Consuelo No. 3255; Magnolia Park No. 715-4; and Oak Plains No. 789-4. Outstanding this year are: Great Lights U.D.-22; ManhattC1n U.D.-11; Frank
S. Land U.D.-10; and Las Palmas No. 366-9.
The following Masonic Districts, which were given honorable mention in 1963. are on the 1964 "hit parade" with 15 Sojourner affiliations
each: Yucaipa No. 605. Lemon Grove No. 638. and La Jolla No. 644.
Outstanding this year are: Van Nuys No. 516-29; San Jose No. 370-27; Burbank No. 520-26; Santa Barbara No. 508-22; El Segundo
No. 584-22; San Diego No. 640-16; and Palo Alto No. 368-15.
The Sixth Division and the State of Hawaii have the distinction of
having at least one Sojourner affiliate in each of their several Lodges.
Each Masonic District, in ·which every Lodge had one or more affiliates,
is given special notation on Exhibit "A."

joumer and other affiliations) is a descending curve. These two curves
practicall y intersect in 1964, when the net Gains were only five.
The Gain Curve shows a slight upward trend in 1964, due to increased Sojourner and other affiliations. This upward trend can be continued by putting increased effort into the Sojourner progra m. We can
do nothing to stop the rise in the Death curve. We can help reduce our
Losses through withdrawals and suspensions by a more liberal inter~
pretation and application of the C.M.C. relative to suspensions fo r nonpayment of dues. We can increase our Gains by aggressive ac tion to
locate Sojourners and sell them on California Masonry. By this double
action we can avoid o r red uce the deficit in our membership that inaction
will produce.
Fear of the examination still keeps many Sojourners from attending
Lodge. We still hear stories of overzealous examining committees that
seem to try to prove how much they know, to the detrime nt of the
Sojourner. Committee members should be instructed not to " throw the
book" but with patience and understanding ascer tain if the applican t is
a Mason and not how much he knows.
Many have suggested that the $25.00 affiliation fee for the Maso nic
Homes be eliminated, as it is a deterrent to affiliations. There may be
some truth to this, but the Sojourner affiliations by Lodges which charge
their own fee hardly bear th is out. Over 350 of o ur Lodges charge from
$1.00 to $75.00 for affiliation. Last year the 25 Lodges with a $25.00
fee affiliated 41 or 1.6 per Lodge; the 13 with a $15.00 fee affiliated 25
or 1.9 per Lodge; the 184 Lodges with a fee of from $1.00 to $9.00 affiliated only 186 or o ne per Lodge as against the overall average of 1.2 .
These figures are surprising and seem to indicate that it is what is offered
that counts rather than the cost. It would hardly be consistent to eliminate the Home fee while so many Lodges have a substantial affi liation
fee and appear to be above average in their Sojourner affiliations. This
matter is worthy of fu r ther study.
It has been suggested that other jurisdictions furnish us w ith the
names and addresses of their Sojourning members. The Sojourner and
his rela ted problems ha ve been discussed at the ann ual Grand Masters'
Conference for years, without specific results. There is no easy solution.
A start might be made if a Lodge Secretary notified the Lodge nea r the
residence of his Sojourning member with a request that he be contacted
and invited to visit. He could also offer to reciprocate. This could become
very involved and cumbersome. It is believed that better and q uicker
results will be obtained if we give public notice of the time and p lace
of our meetings and if we continue to seek out the Sojourner du ring our
everyday activities. A watchful eye for a ring or a pin, follow ed by a
word of greeting and a friend ly invitation to visit will produce s ur prising
results.
The Sojourner program is a continuing one and cannot be solved in

It is disturbing to note that 332 Lodges and 22 Masonic Districts
failed to affiliate a single Sojourner. This is somewhat understandable
in the Mother Lode Country and the sparsely settled mountainous
regions. In the other areas, with our exploding population. it would
appear that the exercise of a little interest and effort would add at least
one Sojourner to the rolls of each Lodge.
It has been said that in the populated metropolitan areas it is more
difficult to secure affiliations than in the smaller communities. A rough
check of the location of the Lodges with the greater number of Sojourner
affiliations indicated somewhat of an equal division between the heavily
and lightly populated areas. This would lead one to the suspicion that
it is the interest and the effort displayed that produces results and not
the population.
Much has been said about the declining membership of this jurisdiction. To present a picture of this decline, the Gain and Loss figures from
the Grand Secretary's Membership Summary have been plotted by year
from 1958 to date. This graph is attached, marked Exhibit "B." The
line showing the Total Losses (deaths, withdrawals, etc.) is an ascending curve. The line showing the Total Gains (raised, reinstated, So-

Sixth: We see no need for more than three members of the Committee on By-Laws and we recommen d that this committee have but three
members and no Senior Warden and Junior Warden members. This
committee provides a technical service only and is restricted in its authority by the provisions of the Uniform Code of By-Laws for Constitue nt
Lodges.
Seventh: We believe there is need of clear-cut, detailed rules of qualifica tion and procedure respecting travel expenses for all Grand Lodge
committee personnel. Not all committee s need an allocation for travel
expenses, but some do. and there should be no lack of understan ding as
to what funds are available and how they are to be spent. We recommend that the Grand Lodge Committe e on Finance be instructed to
develop such rules.

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON
MASON IC INFORM ATION
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
It was my pleasure to report at the Annual Communi cation in September, 1961 the first report of the Committe e on Masonic Informatio n
created at the beginning of that Masonic year by the Grand Master for
1961-1962 . Alfred F. Breslauer. and again at the Annual Communic ation
in October, 1963. Those reports were rather extensive because it seemed
essential to explain to the members of Grand Lodge the reason for the
creation of the Committe e, the importanc e of a comprehen sive program
of Masonic informatio n and the action taken and contempla ted to disseminate truthful and reliable data regarding various Masonic activities.
The Committe e reported last year as follows (Proceedi ngs of the
Grand Lodge of California. 1963. p. 234):
"There are three distinct areas of concern essential to the Public
image of Masonry:
( l ) E ducating the general public;
(2) Keeping Masons informed of the activities of the Grand
Lodge and its constituen t bodies;
( 3) Creating a healthy atmospher e in order to minimize the possibility of adverse criticism."
The Committe e is pleased to report favorable progress in all three
areas. The Grand Lodge, constituen t Lodges and Masons throughou t

243

California and Hawaii have become conscious of the significanc e of
advantage ous communic ation with the genera l public in stimulatin g an
understan ding of the salutary purposes of Masonry and attracting the
interest of prospectiv e members.
The fou r -point program recommen ded in the 1963 Report included
first. the developme nt of a greater measure of concurren t effort by the
Grand Lodge Committe e on Public Informatio n and constituen t lodges
aided by a "Handboo k for Masonic Informatio n" containing techn.ique s
for the conduct of public relations pursuits. and, second. the continued
cooperatio n of the Committe e with the Masonic Press Clubs of Los
Angeles and of Northern California .
The principal achieveme nts of the Committe e during the past year
are:
First: assistance toward the completio n of the organizati on of the
Masonic Press Club of Northern California ; and
Second: the final drafting of the handbook referred to earlier in this
report.
The Masonic Press Club of Los Angeles has been in existence several years and under excellent direction has rendered valuable service
to Masonry by the distributio n to the public media:--ne w.spaper.s. television and radio-of informatio n regarding M asonic affairs of mterest
to the public.
The Masonic Press Club of Northern California was operating de
facto at the time of the 1963 Communic ation: however, it came into
existence officially at its charter installatio n of officers and banquet held
at the Press Club. San Francisco, March 4. 1964. On that occasion the
trustees were installed by Most Worshipf ul Elmer W. Heald. The
organizati on has increased its membersh ip 'substantiall~ and is responsible for the distributio n of numerous press releases during the year and
currently in the newspape rs.
The handbook has been expanded into a "Public Relations Manual "
with the expectatio n that it may prove of valuable use to the constituen t
lodges in the field of public informatio n and result in an enlarged program. The manual soon will be printed and distributed to the lodges of
California and Hawaii.
The manual is designed as a guide principally for the constituen t
lodges in the developm ent of public informatio n programs in their respective communiti es. In the 1963 report of the Committe e it is recommen ded
that Masters of the constituen t lodges should appoint a brother. or a
committee , to conduct the public informatio n effort. It is hoped that the
Masters elected to take office following this Communic ation will make
such appointme nts and actuate the plan in order that an over-all program
in California and Hawaii may be effectuated .

TRIAL RECORD S NOS. 1469 AND 1649
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
In Trial Record No. 1469 a former member of Mount Olive Lodge
No. 506 and in Trial Record No. 1649 a former member of Sequoia
Lodge No. 349, each have petitioned for restoration to the right and
privileges of Masonry.
Section 767 C.M.C. states that the petition for restoration must be
submitted in writing to the Lodge from which the accused was expelled
at least sixty days before the Annual Communi cation at which his petition is to be presented.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

248

249

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

In Trial Record No. 1469 the petition was ·s ubmitted to the Lodge. 011
Septembe r 3. 1964. and in Trial Record N o. 1649 the petition was submitted to the Lodge on Septembe r I . 1964.
The petitions in these two trial records were not submitted within the
sixty day period.
We. therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLV ED: That the petitions for restoration in Trial Records
No. 1469 and 1649 be denied.
Adopted .

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1819

To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
The accused. a member of Liberty Lodge No. 299, was convicted of
murder in the State Courts and committed to prison. Notice of intended
expulsion under Section 732 C.M.C. was given. He wrote a letter to
the Lodge, which amounted to a demand for a trial and it was treated
as such. Later after his friends and relatives. who visited him at the
prison, had shown him the futility of having a trial in the Lodge. he
withdrew the demand. The Master at the next Stated Meeting declared
him expelled.
Where notice of intended expulsion is given and a demand for trial
is made. and the 60 day period expires, the power of the Lodge to
expel is ended and no withdrawa l of the demand for trial may be made
after said period. The Lodge must proceed to serve notice under Section
692.l C.M.C .. and to investigat e the charge or to have a trial before a
Commission if necessary.
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLV ED : That the purported expulsion of the accused in Trial
Record No. 1819 be reversed and set aside and the matter remanded to
the Lodge with direction to proceed to have charges filed and proper
proceedin gs taken thereon.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1825

To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A member of a Kentucky Lodge sojourning within the jurisdictio n
of Downey Lodge No. 220 was charged in tha t Lodge with improper
associatio n with the wife of a Master Ma'5on. He pleaded not guilty and
was tried by a Commission, which found him guilty. The Commissi on
apparently felt that the facts proved justified a finding of guilt but tha t
the penalty of suspension was sufficient, and it so directed. The result
seems proper.
Being suspended by the Lodge. the accused will be entitled to apply
to it for restoration if he ever sees fit to do so but. should the Lodge vote
restoration by a two-thirds ballot. he will not be restored to any Lodge in
California but only to the rights and privileges of Masonry in this

'urisdiction. If Kentucky has suspended or expelled him, restoration
~ re would not affect his status there and he would be a Mason at la~ge
o:ly and. should he apply for affiliation in California . his then sta nding
in Kentucky should be investigate d .
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLV ED : That the finding of guilt and suspension of the
accused in Trial Record No. 1825 be ratified , affirmed and approved.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1835
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California :

The accused was charged in Phoenix Lodge No. 178 in M ay. 1962.
with various a llegations, the basic one being the use of a false and
assumed name when petitioning that Lodge for affiliation. It was also
charged that he had been indicted in an United States District Court
for falsifying his name on a passport applicatio n. (This indictmen t was
later dismissed by the Federal Court on the ground that accused had
.
acted in good faith. )
The charges were amended and a trial '-Vas had before a commission late in 1963, accused found guilty of using a false name and suspended. The proceedin gs were somewhat irregular in that the trial
took place before commissio ners elected over a year before.
However, the main problem in the case is whether the use of a name
other than that of his father was unmasonic conduct. Willful use of a n
assumed name in a petition has been held improper in Section 526d.
Masonic Code. but Section 526e holds that the adoption of a name
without intention to injure others was not a Masonic offense.
In the instant case the surna me of the father of the accused was
foreign-so unding , and early in life he adopted a shorter and simpler
name, and used it for years in all his activities. such as his Social
Security papers, his record as a civilian employee of the Air Force.
and in many other ways. He used his new name exclusivel y.
In almost all. if not all, States there is a Court procedure for changing names by which a record of such change can be made, but it is also
the law that anyone may adopt a new name without any Court procedure .
if it is not with intent to defraud or for some unlawful or improper
purpose.
We hold, therefore, that the conduct of the accused was not wrong
nor unmasonic in any way and the evidence does not support the finding
of guilt. There is no reason for retrying this case.
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLV ED : That the finding of guilt of the accused and his suspension by Phoenix Lodge No. l 78 be reversed ;md ~et aside. that a
6nding o f not guilty be substitute d and the ch~rge against th e accused
be dismissed .
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1839
To the M ost Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California :
A member of Montebell o Lodge No. 451 was charged with writing
and circulating among Masons a letter which slandered and defamed
the Brethren of the Jewis h faith belonging to the Masonic Fraternity
and did advocate that the Masonic Fraternity be limited to white
Christians .
After a trial by Whittier Lodge No. 323. at the direction of the
Grand Master, before a commission he was found guilty and ordered
reprimand ed.
Your Committe e feels that the charges of which the member was
found guilty are of grave nature in that they contraven e one of our
basic principles and philosoph y and that the penalty should be raised
to expulsion.
We. therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLV ED : That the finding of guilty in Trial Record No. 1839
be approved but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that the
accused be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

EMERG ENT RESOLU TION
The Commitbee on Grievances:
Your Committe e on Grievance s to which was referred the resolution
to relieve West Gate Lodge No. 335 of the duty of trying two Brothers
of that Lodge, reports as follows:
If Grand Lodge sets a precedent by grantin g \,Yest Gate Lodge
No. 335 this relief it may start a rush of such applicatio ns each year

251

and Grand Lodge will be busy trying charges during its Annual Communication . The Lodge, in this case . has charges on file separately for
the two Brothers who were convicted by plea of grand theft, a felony.
The Lodge should proceed with these charges in the proper manner.
Charges which do not involve a criminal act may be withdrawn by
the accuser before trial. but where crimes. such as grand theft, are
charged there is no authorizat ion in our law for wit hdrawal or dismissal.
Grand Lodge has wisely delegated the power to its Lodges to pass
on the merits of charges and the guilt or innocence of those charged, and
should not itself undertake to decide whether an accused is guilty or not.
We recommen d against adoption of this resolution .
The Committe e on Jurisprudence:
The Committe e on Jurisprude nce indicated its concurren ce in the
recommen dation.
Adopted.

tish Rite Bodies bulletins- The Los Angeles Shrine Bulletin, California
Freemason, Pot of Gold, The Cordon, and in the Trestle Boards of some
Masonic lodges. More publicity was given at various Masonic functions
by speakers and by displays.
The Board thanks their Masonic Brethren for this publicity as it is
only by constant telling of our story that membersh ip is developed .
During the spring semester a building was erected next door on
Bancroft. It was necessary for us to obtain the services of an architect
to assist us in this matter. It also was necessary to shore up our foundation at great expense to the Clubhouse .
The constructi on rules and regulation s were generally observed but
dama ge was done to the interior of the building. At first glance the damage appeared to be very heavy but, after checking , the architect determined that no serious damage had resulted and our costs were below
$1.000. Our total costs approxima ted $6,000-p aid from capital.
A very effective sign has been erected at the front of the building.
This was pa rt of our promotion al program and has received much favorable comment.
Tile appropria tion granted us by Grand Lodge amounted to $22.850
-of this amount we expended $21,786.35.
Several items of expense were not taken care of before the end of the
fiscal year due to the constructi on next door and the resultant dust and
dirt.
It is our desire that as many of the members of Grand Lodge as possible visit our building oi:i their return from the Union City visit.
Your Board of Directors consider it an honor and privilege to serve
Masonry in this manner and hope that through our contact with the boys
at California we may develop in them an interest in Masonry.
In conclusion . the Directors wish to thank the hostesses, student officers and members for their excellent cooperatio n during the past year.
Respectfu lly submitted ,

BERKELEY, CALIFO RNIA
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
The Berkeley Clubhouse Board of Directors submits herewith its
report for the year ending July 31, 1964.
A word of thanks must be conveyed to the Grand Master Elmer W.
Heald and the officers of Grand Lodge for their interest and understan ding of the problems which are associated with the campus of a large
university . The directors, hostesses and students have worked together
to build up the membersh ip and in handling the various problems which
have arisen during the past year.
A very energetic promotion al program was carried out during the
past year. Over that period of time there were held various affairs to
aid this program such as a Fall Friendship Dinner, a Breakfast and
Victory Dinner. in addition to the regularly scheduled open house for
students.
The result of these activities is shown by the increase in membersh ip
from 51 as of Septembe r 10, 1963, to 176 on June I, 1964. This was 24
short of our goal of 200 which we promised Grand Master Coburn. We
shall continue to work together to build the membersh ip.
Other affairs to promote the membersh ip drive were planned , but
due to a full program prepared by the students prior to ours these were
not carried out. They are part of the 1964-65 promotion al program.
Last year a film was prepared by one of the students assisted by past
and present members. This film ha s been shown by many Blue Lodges
and Masonic organizat ions-both youth and adult. Also, Fresno State
College requested the use of the film and it was well received there. It
also will be shown at Grand Lodge during the Communic ations.
A brochure was prepared and sent to all members of the California
jurisdictio n. In addition, publicity has been given in many of the Scot-

CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE TAX

Masonic lodges will be subject to this tax if the total wages paid
during a calendar quarter to taxable employees are in excess of $100.
For this purpose a taxable employee is one who is paid $50 or more per
calendar quarter. However, whether or not elected or appointed officials
of a lodge are to be counted as taxable employees will depend upon
whether or not the lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax
Act.
If the lodge is not subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act,
then the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be exempt
from the California Unemployment Insurance Tax unless the wages paid
to these officials exceed $100 per month.
If the lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, then
the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be subject to
California Unemployment Insurance Tax if the wages paid to these
officials amount to $50, or more, per calenda r quarter.
For purposes of this tax, the term "elected or appointed official" will
include any official of the lodge who is compensated for his services.
Those usually compensated for their services are the Secretary, Tiler,
Organist, and Soloist.
If the lodge is subject to the California Unemployment Insurance
Tax, the tax rate shown below will be applicable to the first $3,800 paid
to each employee during the calendar year 1965. Only the employer pays
the tax.
Rates based on employment experience ,

Ne il M arion Ousley. a Brother held in very high regard in San Bernardino, entered into rest on May 28. 1964. Brother Ousley was a mem~
her of Damascus Lodge No. 648. being raised on January 26, 193 1, and
serving as its M aster in 1954. For a number of yea rs he served as Sec~
retary. holding that office at the time o f his dea th. He was amongst those
who have raised sons as Ma ster Masons. and he assisted in conferring
the degrees on three brothers, all of whom are now Past Masters, his
son-in-law, and five nephews. O ne of his brothers. Joseph L. Ousley.
is now Inspector of District No. 602 . A member of the Baptist Church,
he was active in many departmen ts of his Church. Always interested in
young people, he was Chairman of the Rainbow Assembly Board and
was also Chairman of the Youth C ommittee for the Sciots in 1962,
when he was voted the outstandin g "Sciot of the Year" by the S upreme
Assembly. When he died he was scheduled to receive public honors for
his service to a school for retarded children. He spent countless hours
ministerin g to the welfare of these young people a nd children. As a fi tting tribute to this fine Mason . over four hundred people attended his
funer al conducted by Damascus Lodge. Being a " Bridge and Building
Foreman." at his fu neral his Minister said , "While he built bridges of
steel. in his daily life he built bridges of gold in the hearts a nd lives of
his fellow men."
We rejoice that he has been part of our fellowship and we believe he
has heard his Master' s " V./ell done. good and faithful serva nt. enter
into the joy of thy Lord."
Robert/-/. T aylor was raised in the Celestial Lodge on July 14. 1964,
at the comparati vely early age of sixty one years.
Bob was East Bay from beginning to end. He was born in Oakland
in April. 1903, and died in Berkeley. He attended Oakland Technical
High School. w here he was a classmate of Inspector E. Lloyd H ansen
with whom he was a close friend to the end of his days. H e graduated
from University of C alifornia Dental School in 1924. He practiced fo r
a while in O akland, then opened an office in Albany. where he continued to practice to the time of his death. He ha d a career of distinguis hed
service in Masonry. A member of H enry M orse Stephens Lodge No.
541 , he was raised on Jan uary 27, 1943. and served that Lodge as Master in 1948. He became Inspector of District No. 348 in October, 1949.
and continued in that office until D ecember. 1960. H e was a Past President of East Bay M aste rs a nd Wardens Associa tion a nd served as
President o f M asters and P ast M asters Associatio n of Alameda and
Contra Costa Counties. D uring the years Bob served on various Grand
Lodge Committe es.

272

Music was his avocatio n. He was a skilled musician and played the
piccolo, Bute, clarinet and saxophon e. He had been a member of Oakland Boys' Band, Bohemia n Club Band, Scottish Rite Orchestr a, and
Aahmes Temple Shrine Band.
He was dentist for the former Oakland Baseball Team and was a
member of the Sportsm en's Club of Albany.
While Robert Taylor was a man of wide interests a nd many activities. he was also a genial. kindly. warm-he arted person. Many of us
will remembe r him longest for his warm friendliness. and we are thankful we were privileged to enjoy fellowship with him. Our sincerest sympathy goes out to his wife and daughter s.
There are many names on the list which is a part of this report. One
Brother. Leonard Arthur Walton of Enterpri se Lodge No. 70. was one
of the oldest members of this Grand Lodge. He was raised on March
26. 1892. and served as Master of his Lodge in 1897. He was a member
of this Grand Lodge for at least sixty six years. There are the names
oI men who served on school boards, city councils , and a t least one who
served for many years as Mayor of his city. There are some whose
integrity in public life and in business added lustre to the name of
Mason. All those on the list served their Lodges for many years and
helped to make Masonry a respected title in the land. We honor them
for it, and are thankful to God that we enter into their labors.
"We shall ever cherish in our hearts the memory of our departed
Brothers and, commending their spirits to Almighty God. we trustingl y
leave them in the hands of that Beneflcient Being who has done all
things well; who is glorious in His Holiness . wondrou s in His power
and boundles s in His goodness ; and it should always be our endeavor
so to live that we, too. may be found worthy to inherit the kingdom
prepared for us from the foundati on of the world."

"CALIFO RNIA FREEMA SON"

The Commit tee on Policy and General Purpos es :
Referra l has been made to the Commit tee on Policy and General
Purpose s of that portion of the Grand Master' s Messag e in which he
recomm ends that the Grand Lodge establis h a policy of send ing the
California Freemason , at Grand Lodge expense , to every member.
The Grnnd Master has said that "it is his firm belief that by placing
in the hands of every Master Mason in the Californ ia Grand Lodge
would be doing a great service to Masonr y and would do much toward
inspirin g and encoura ging every Master Mason to work harder and
more earnestly for the good of our great Fratern ity."
The Commit tee approve d last year a similar recomm endatio n and
it sees no reason to change that opinion .
We move the approva l of the recomm endatio n and your Commit tee
recomm ends a yes vote.
The Commit tee on Finan ce:
There has been referred to this Commit tee the recomm endatio n of
the Grand Master that our official magazin e, California Freemason. be
mailed to all Masons of this jurisdic tion who are regular member s of our
Lodges , with the cost to be borne by Grand Lodge.
This matter was before Grand Lodge last year on the recomm enda tion of the Grand Master and. in the form of resoluti ons, on a number
in
of occasio ns in the past. Grand Lodge has defeate d the proposa l
case.
every
Your decision rests on one simple but importa nt point: Do you. as
the represen tatives of your Lodges, wish to spend the money to put the
proposa l into operatio n? We estimate that your per capita will have to be
increase d a minimum of 25 cents to do so. An addition al s um will have
to be spent by Grand Lodge to prepare address ograph plates for all
the members.
The decision rests in your hands.
Adopte d.

PuBuc ScHOOLs WEEK CoMMITTEE-DEFINITION OF RESPONSIBILITY
(4)
The Commit tee on Policy and General Purposes:
There has been referred to the Commi ttee on Policy and Genera l
Purpose s Resolut ion No. 4, entitled "Public Schools Week Commit tee
-Defin ition of Respon sibility, " which seeks to amend Section 331
C.M.C. by adding a paragra ph thereto, to read: "That each constitu ent
Lodge of this jurisdiction appoint a 'Commi ttee on Public Schools ' to
actively work with the Boards of Educati on, (one or more members to
attend meeting s of the School Boards} , faculty and/or other official
organiz ations of the Public Schools. That this committee report to each
Stated Meeting of their respecti ve Lodges, and that each Lodge make
a quarter ly report to Grand Lodge. That there be a report of these
committees publish ed for each communication of Grand Lodge."
The Grand Lodge of Californ ia, its constitu ent Lodges, and Masons ,
as individu als, have been known -and known favorab ly-for many
years as support ers of a strong public school system. Our support has
redound ed favorab ly for the cause of the Public Schools and those who
are engage d in the educati ng of our children, the teachers , adminis trators, members of Boards of Educati on. Our support to date, in the direction it has taken, has likewise redound ed favorab ly to our Fratern ity.
It is the opinion of this Commi ttee that aside from the conside rable
amount of time and effort which would have to be expende d by individual members, Lodge secretar ies and the Grand Secreta ry's ·staff, to
implement the physical aspects of this amendm ent, the value of the
reports to be made and compiled into an annual report for each communicat ion of Grand Lodge might well be negligible by reason of wide
diversities at every step in the total suggest ed procedu re.
Of greater concern to th~s Commi ttee is our belief that attempt ing to
place watcher s by the dozens, even hundred s in the larger metropo litan
areas, at the various types of meeting s propose d in this resolution, would
bring down charges of politics on our heads and the good wrough t by
our efforts over the years in support of free public schools could well be
destroy ed in short order. Masons , as individu al citizens of the community, should be interest ed in support ing the objectives implied in this
resolution. This Is a position long advocat ed by this Grand Lodge.
Howeve r, we cannot recomm end that the activities propose d be made
a part of our Grand Lodge program of support of public schools.
We present the resoluti on for action but strongly urge a no vote.
The Commit tee on Public Schools:
The Commi ttee on Public Schools agrees that Masonr y's support
of the principle of free public educatio n is a 52 week job every year
rather than a one week celebration.
This Commi ttee agrees that the program of the Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools must constan tly be strength ened: that new

ELIMINATE HOMES CONTRIBUTION BY AFFILIATES
(2)
The Commit tee on Policy and General Purposes:
your Commi ttee on Policy and Genera l Purpose s has carefull y
conside red Resolut ion No. 2 which propose s to delete that part of Se~­
tion 284 C.M.C. requirin g paymen t of the contributio~ t~ t~e .Masonic
Homes of Californ ia by sojourn ing brethre n from other 1urisd1ctions who
apply for affiliation with a Lodge in this jurisdiction.
.
Each petition er to form a new L?dg~ and eac~ applica~t for the
deg·rees is required to make this contribu tion and this. Res~l~tion would
create a distinct ion among brethre n by grantin g a special privilege to one
group which would not be extende d to others.
The Masoni c Homes of Californ ia are support ed by all of our members as our greates t charity and it is the opini~n of ~our Commi ttee that
no sojourn ing brother should hesitate to affiliate with us because they
were required to make this contribu tion.
These contribu tions are not placed in the Endowm ent Fund, but are
used for the operatio n of the Homes and the thousan.ds of dol~ars which
would be lost to the Homes by the adoptio n of this resoluti on would
have to be recover ed by an increase in "the per capita tax on all Lodges.
We move the resoluti on and recomm end a no vote.
The Commit tee on furisprucknce:

.
The Resolut ion relating to contribu tions to the Masom c Homes is:

a contribu tion of $25.00 for the use and benefit of the Masoni c Homes
of Californ ia.
The effect of this change would be to exempt all affiliates from payment of the $25.00. This is unrealis tic and unfair to applica nts for the
degrees .
This same resoluti on was present ed by the same Brother last year
and soundly defeate d.

it again.

Even motorists rail at the pollution of our outdoors by billboards. signs
and other symbols of commercial sprawl. Because of this scorn, the cost
of such commercial advertising and the present speed of the would-be
readers on the highways. some advertisers are removing their signboards
from the highways.
1. Passage of this resolution would plunge Masonry into this controversy. It would drop the great name and fame of Masonry to the street
level with commercial advertising.
We move adoption of the resolution as presented but urge a no vote.
The Committee on Finance reported but without recommendation.
A simple majority voted for the resolution. Failing a 5/6 vote. the
matter was held over until the 1965 Annual Communication as a "Proposed Amendment to the Ordinances." (Sec. 783 C.M.C.)
PUBLISH NAMES OF ELECTED CANDIDATES

(7)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 7 has been referred to your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes. and we have carefully considered it.
This resolution proposes an amendment to Section 331 of the California Masonic Code. The amendment would permit a Lodge to notify
its members in its Trestleboard. or other document sent through the
United States mail. of the names of applicants for the degrees in that
Lodge. and in like manner. of the names of Candidates scheduled to
receive a degree upon a particular night.
It must be borne in mind that the proposed amendment is permissive
and not mandatory. If adopted, it would permit each Lodge to decide
for itself whether it would use one or both such notices. or neither of
them. At present. no Lodge may make a choice of the course it follows.
because all Lodges are prohibited from using either notice.
As stated a moment ago. the fir st portion of the proposed amendment
would grant permission to a Lodge to notify its members through the
mail of the names of applicants for the Degrees in that Lodge. Probably
many of you have seen. as we have, notices of this type emanating
from some English. Canadian. or Australian Lodge. or from a Lodge in
some other Jurisdiction in the United States. We have seen such notices
in Trestlebonrds. and on other occasions in a separate folded sheet
enclosed with other mailed matter. Under the proposed amendment.
each Lodge which determined to gi\·e notice could determine the form
of the notice, whether in the Trestleboard, or by separate enclosure.
It should be pointed out that the proposed amendment contemplates
a notice which would not be as broad as some we have seen, for it
speaks only of giving the names of applicants. while some from other
Jurisdictions we have seen give not only the name of the applicant. but
his address and occupation.

303

It is .reasonably certain that some opponent of the proposed amendexpress the fear that some profane, somewhere, sometime,
will .see the name of an applicant and it may be suggested that some
applicant may be solicited to buy something. The very fact that our
proposed notice would not carry an address or occupation would seem
to be a safeg~ard against any commercial use of the notice by anyone.
One obvious and valuable purpose of sending the names of applicants for the Degrees to the me mbers of the Lodge receivinri the applic~tion :voul~ be to alert any member who possessed knowl~dge of the
d1squ~lificat1on of an applicant. He could then come fonvard and protect his Lodge from the election of an unworthy applicant. Under our
present system. the only way all the members of any Lodge can know
the names of all applicants for the Degrees is for every member of the
Lodg~ . no rnatt~r where he resides. to attend every alternate Stated
Meeting. There is not a single Lodge in this Jurisdiction where that will
happen or be approximated.
Answer to yourselves the question: Have unworthy applicants been
admitted to our Lodges because the re was no practical machinery to
alert members who possessed knowledge of their unworthiness?
Answer to yourselves the question: Isn't it possible that this proposed procedure might contribu te to the reduction of the number of
Masonic trials with which this Jurisdiction is saddled every year?
Answer two further questions: Are our Lodges so ashamed of the
name of some applicant that they must leave all their members not
present in the hall in the ~ark as to the names of all applicants to prevent
some profane from learnmg the fact that a certain application has been
made? To which do you attach the most importance, the protection of
your Lodge or the fear that a profane will see a name of an app licant?
.There is a second valuable and more pleasant purpose which a
notice of the names of applicants will serve. That is to alert a member
who is a friend or acquain tance of an applicant that the applicant is
about to knock at the door of the Lodge. Such a notice would appear
to be a courtesy by the Lodge to such a member. Would not such a
notice be appreciated by those members of your Lodge who are not as
regular in their attendance as you are?
Let us turn now to the second part of the proposed amendme nt. It
would permit a Lodge, if it decided so to do. to notify its members in its
Tre~tleboard, or by other document sent through the mail. that on a
particular night a candidate or candidates named in the notice would
receive a Degr~e. Such advance notice also partakes of a courtesy from
the Lodge to its members. It would advise all the friends of all the
Candidat~s scheduled for a particular night of the coming conferrals,
and permit them to arrange their personal calendars to avoid conflicts
and attend. How often, in how many Lodges, we ask, does a membe~
miss a Degree conferred on a friend-or mere acquaintance-because he

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

door-far outweighs any possible financial gains that would accrue to
our ~dges or to other organizations requiring Ma sonic affiliation as a
condition of membership.
W,,c doubt very much that "Masonry has substantially suffered"
from the loss of respectable revenue," as recited in the third paragraph
of the preamble of this resolution. What loss any so-called affiliated
organization may have sustained by reason of Section 334 is not a
concern of this Grand Lodge.
The ~roponents ~a.ve attempted to guard against abuses by limiting
the permitted advertisin9 by the lan9uage quoted in the above second
paragraph. That language, however, is so vague and indefinite as to be
impossible of enforcement: who could with any certainty determine
that an ad "might" or "might not" "prove to be less than beneficial to
any person who might be" persuaded to buy the product advertised?
This Committee. therefore. moves the adoption of Resolution No. 9
but recommends a no vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
There has been presented to the Committee on Jurisprudence a proposed Resolution No. 9 to amend Section 334 of the C.M.C. by permitting Masonic advertising. unless it would bring discredit on Masonry
or prove nonbeneficial or misleading.
Your Committee feels the proposed resolution would emasculate
the protective provisions of our present law on the subject. We remind
t~e Gra.nd Lodge that this present law was born of abuses that did bring
d1scred1t on Masonry and that did prove nonbeneficial and misleading
to those induced by such advertising. The sorry story is reflected in
reports of Committees of this Grand Lodge over years past. Pursuant
to recommendatio ns of your Grand Lodge Committees. reported in our
proceedings. the Grand Lodge adopted our present law in 1951, and
further strengthened the law in 1954. The abuses of which some unscrupulous individuals and publications were guilty brought disgrace to
the good name of Masonry. Those abuses were cleared up and the good
name of Masonry was restored on the strength of our present Jaws.
Any interested brother need only read the Committee reports to catch
a glimpse of why we need the law in its present form and why there
should be no such amendment as proposed. See, for example. our proceedings of 1951, page 131: and of 1954. page 148. Your Grand Lodge,
as recommended by your Grand Lodge Committees. authorized litigation which was conducted on behalf of Grand Lodge successfully, and
which resulted in a judgment in favor of Grand Lodge to forbid the
use of Masonic names and symbols in advertising and for fraudulent
purposes. A copy of the judgment is set forth on pages 371 and 372
C.M.C.
The proposed amendment would again lead to abuses. It would be
the foot in the door for exploiters and promoters of advertising and

advertising publications to commercialize Masonry. For exai:i~le. it
contains no method for adequate policing of the type of advert1~mg or
for surveillance of the publication. nor is there any safeguard agamst the
usual commercial implications . Moreover. our experience has ·s hown that
such policing and surveillance is not practicable. 1:'he proposed amend~
ment would permit a person to advertise in Masonic channels for monetary gain to himself. That is contrary to Masonic concepts. The person
runn ing such an ad would subject the Craft to the danger of a recurre~ce
of those abuses which plagued this Grand Lodge before the protection
of our present law. and if it be argued that the person who wo.uld so
advertise was not doing so for monetary gain to himself alon: m that
there might be incidental benefits or gain to a Lodge. then this should
be weighed against opening a door to unscrupulous persons and to the
overwhelming fraud that your Committees found always grew and
festered in similar types of advertising.
We. therefore, move adoption of the resolution but urge a no. vote .
The Committee on Commercialism indicated its concurrence m the
recommendatio n.
A majority voted against the resolution.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS

( 16)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Nearly every year we have had one or more resolution s attempting
to change the requirements of physical qualifications or to abolis h them ,
and this year is no exception.
Resolution No. 16 seeks to break down the existing law by adding
to Section 512 C.M.C. a proviso that " Joss o f the left forearm would
not constitute physically disqualifying an applicant for the degrees of
M asonry"; that is, to provide an exception for a particular case.
All of these proposals to change the physical requirements. often
considered as an Ancient Landmark, have been evoked by a natural
sympathy for those unfortunate men who have suffered severe physical
injuries. It was that sympathy which caused the compromise many
years ago which. resulted in the adoption of our pres~nt regula~ions.
contained in Sections 511 and 512 of the C.M.C.: having no maim or
defect in his body that may render him incapable of learning the art.
and physically able to conform substantially to what the several degrees
respectively require of him." The question as to physical sufficiency of
the applicant is left to the sound discretion of the Lodge. and it is
necessarily determined by the ritual- he must be able to conform substantially to the ritual.
The proponents do not claim. and they certainly cannot claim. that
a candidate who has lost his left forearm can comply or substantially
comply with our ritual. We all know that he cannot.
We do not think that a change should be made in the law to meet
one particular case of ineligibility. It would simply lead to demands for
exceptions in other cases in which an ap plicant cannot comply with our
requirements.
Masonry selects its candidates. No one has a right to admission. It
is a privilege granted to a comparatively small number of men and our
law has fixed the tests of eligibility. This Grand Lodge made a reasonable compromise on the question of physical qualification and we see no
reason to go further. The degrees cannot be conferred in a purely symbolic manner and the candidate must be able to conform substantially
to what the ritual requires of him.
We disapprove the resolution and urge a no vote.
The Committee on furisprudence:
This resolution seeks to amend Sec. 512 C.M.C. by adding at the end
thereof the following:
"The loss of the left forearm would not constitute physically
disqualifying an applicant for the degrees of Masonry.''
Under our law the following physical defects disqualify an
applicant:

GRAND LODGE O P CALIFORNl1\

315

Loss of a foot, loss of right hand. loss of leg . and loss of an eye and
· · 1eg. (513-hC.M.C.).
· Loss of left forearm would ten d to disqua lify to a greater extent
·
·
than mos t of the defects cited.
This resolutio n would violate Landmark Eightccnth- -"The qualification of candidates for initiation ." ( C.M.C. p. 343) and the Un written
Law-"A candidate must be without blemish and have the full and
proper use of his limbs; . .. " (Article 5, p. 314 C.M.C.).
Every year of late, resolutions to reduce the physical qu:ilifications
of applicants have come before this Grand Lodge and all have been
defeated by votes of the brethre n. Similar resolu tion s Nos. 7 & 8 were
defeated in 1961; No. 5 "vils rejected in 1962 and No. 15 was defeated in
1963.
This resolut ion s hould also be defeated. \Ve move adoption of the
resolution as presented but urge a no vote.
The Committee on Rit11al indicated its concurrence in the recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution .
EXTEND STATEWIDE TERRITORIAL }URISDICTION TO ALL L ODG ES

( 17)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The purposes of th is resolution. as stated in the resolution itself. are
to give statewide territor ial jurisdiction to all Lodges, to .ibolish the l 0
mile limit and the requirement of notice to other Lodges. and the necessity for waivers of jurisdiction . T o illustrate the result. a man residing
in San Diego could make application for the degrees to a Lodge in
Eureka without notification to any other Lodge, and vice versa. The
resolution seeks to repeal four sections of our law relating to jurisdiction
of Lodges and to amend two others. and to requ ire the Code Commission
to eliminate dozens of annotations.
The proponents of this resolution argue that the presen t requirements
cause delay, and that the Lodge receiving the application "through
proper dilig ence could safely investigate the applicant."
The present requirements a re based upon the sound principle that
the people amonH whom a man lives can best judge his eligibility and
qualifications. The requirements are not, as the proponents assume,
merely to protect Lodges from "poaching" by other Lodges. I3ut if the
provisions have some protective features. the proponents say that a n
active, vir ile Lodge doesn't need any protection. If you are not an active.
virile Lodge, then apparently you are not entitled to protection.
The fact that the present procedure is slow is advantageous, becau se
it permits more time for investigation and for obtaining information
concerning a pplicants.
One of the most frequent criticisms throughout the years has been
the lack of throughness in the inves tigation of candidates. We com-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this matter has not been paid. We recommend that the payment of this
fee be authorized and that it be charged to the capital account of Grand

are $3.00 or higher. The average per capita for all forty nine jurisdictions
is $3.13 which compares with the per capita in California for the last
fi scal year of $3.35.

PER CAPITA SuRvEY-MAso N1c HoMES

In 1959 this Committee. in its report to you, reviewed the per capita
for the previous thirty years. We have brought these figures up-to-date
a nd think it timely to give you some comparisons, not only on the per
capita, but on increased costs as well during this thirty five year period.
Referring only to that portion of the annual per capita paid for the
support of the ordinary activities of Grand Lodge, which includes the
Homes. the low for this thirty five year period was 85 cents in 1946 and
1947. The high was $2.35 in 1963. The average for the period is $1.69.
It should be noted that the 85 cent low in 1946-47 included nothing
for the Homes. The Trustees had been able to build a surplus during
the preceding war years due to the restricted supply of all materials available for purchase.
Including the additional per capita voted from time to time for such
purposes as the University Clubhouses, our Centennial, the George
W ashing ton Ma~onic M emorial and, in recent years. our Memorial
T emple. the low total per capita \vas $1.00 in 1946 and the high was
$3.35 in 1963. The average for the period is $2.1 3.
Perhaps you would be interested in what it has cost per capitawise to
support the activities of Gra nd Lodge alone during this period , without
including the Homes or any of the special purposes. From 1929 to 1936
inclusive the annual per capita was 50 cents, which is the Constitutional
provision. In succeeding years additional per capitas for the support of
Grand Lodge have been voted. The total for Grand Lodge in 1963.
and the high for the thirty five year period, was $1.35. The average per
capita for the period is 92 cents. so that the figure for 1963 is a n
increase of 43 cents over the average. or 46.7 %.
As stated, the total per capita for the last fiscal year was $3.35. This
is made up of $1.00 for the Memorial T emple. $1.00 for the Homes.
and $1.35 for the expenses of Grand Lodge. Deducting the $1.00 for
the Memorial Temple. the remainder of $2.35 for the ordinary activities
o f Grand Lodge is 66 cents above the thirty five year average of $1.69.
or 39.4 % .
We have made a survey of the per capita tax in each of the forty
nine Grand Lodge jurisdictions in the United States. The result is very
enlightening and is of interest to all of us.
Fifteen jurisdictions have a per capita higher than California, ranging
from $3.40 to $8.75. There are three with the low per capita of $1.50 and
these three do not maintain Homes. The remaining thirty one jurisdictions have per capita ranging from $2.00 to $3.35, of which almost half

329

We have also made a survey of assessments for Masonic Homes
or other for ms of charity. Of the forty nine jurisdictions. thirty five
include in their per capita an a mount for •s upport of Masonic charity.
Of these thirty-five. twenty eight maintain homes for adults or children ,
or both. The am ount of assessment ranges from 20 cents to a high of
$6.25. The average for the thirty five jurisdictions is $1. 50. which compares with $1.00 in California for our H omes for the last fiscal year.
You can draw your own conclusion, but it seems a ppropriate at
this point to emphasize that we in California a re on the middle ground
in the a rea of what we pay to support our H omes a nd Grand Lodge.
In view of our comparative size, the wide scope of the Grand Lodge
program. and the acknowledged leadership which California shares in
the M asonic W orld , we think you can take some satisfaction in the
fact that we support this at a compartively reasonable cost.
A statistical survey recently made shows that the 1939 dollar is
today worth 40 cents. Stated another way, this simply mea ns that in the
last twenty five years the cost of goods and services which your dollar
can buy has more than doubled-much more.
If you will refer to the figures on per capita for the period which we
surveyed above, you will reca ll that the per capita for ordinary expenses
of Grand Lodge-which includes the Home assessment-has increased
only 39.4% over.the average for the period. We have been able to hold
down this increase only beca use the number of members paying the per
capita has grown substantially in this twen ty five year period.
This membe rship growth has tapered off a lar mingly in the last several
years, however. and further complicates our problem of bala ncing the
budget, unless this trend is reversed.
The most striking comparison we can give you in reference to per
capita versus expense in this period has to do with the Homes. In 1939
total expense for operating the Homes was $272.958.00. In 1963 this
figure was $1 .489,085.00. an increase of 445 %-. By comparison your per
capita for the H omes in 1939 was 90 cents. In 1963 it was $1 .00. an
increase o f 11 %. There are two fundamental reasons why you have
not had to match these increased costs with a corresponding per capita
increase. The first, and main rea,s on is the income from the Endowment
Fund which has grown because of your gifts. All this income is used
to support the H omes. The second is because of the foresight of the
Trustees in building an unappropriated reserve out of which operating
deficits have been paid from time to time, and for the last three years
total deficits in excess of $800.000.00. This has reduced the reserve

We have followed our usual practice of conferring with all Chairmen of Committees and Boards who require appropriations. Several of
these have requested larger appropriations to implement expanded
programs which have the enthusiastic support of the Gra nd Master
and the Deputy Grand Master, and which have been outlined in reports
given to you. The Deputy Grand Master met with this Committee for
a discussion of his plans for the coming year. As a result of these conferences we have been able to reduce some appropriations but not enough
to offset the increases mentioned above.
Although the proposed budget is in balance, it leaves only a small
margin for emergencies which may and usually do arise. However, we
are not proposing any increase in the per capita for the support of Grand

EULOGY
CHESTER HARVEY WARLO W

By Les lie E. Wo od

MAS O NIC MEMORIAL SERVICE
A Masonic Me moria l Service was conducted for Past Grand Master
Chester Harvey Warlow at 2:00 p.m. Thursday. December 12, 1963. in
the Scottish Rite Temple. 1455 L Street. Fres no. Past Grand Master
Arthur M. Warren presided as Master, Pas t Gra nd Master Ed ward H .
Siems acted as Chaplain , and Past Grand M aster Leslie E. W ood gave
the Eulogy which is appended to this account.
The following Past M asters of Fresno Lodge No. 247 were active
pa llbearers:
Richard D . Heppner
Donald L. Anderson
Ralph W. Kue ttel
Wayne H. Towne
Lester M. Grimm
John L. Stewart
All Inspectors General Honorary 33° of the Fresno Scottis h Rite
Bodies were designated as honorary pallbearers.
A Masonic Graveside Ceremon y concluded the service.

Looking back over a period of 111 ore than thirty years of close
friendship and associa tio n with Chester Harvey Warlow, it is \Nith a
feeling o f sadness and inadeq uacy that I attempt to pay this last tribute
to his memory.
Chester H arvey Warlow. or "Chet .. as he preferred to be called and
was known to hi s many friends. hetd that rare ability to make peopl e
feel corn for table in his presence and at the fir st mee ti ng to create the
feeling that they had been friend s of long standing. As a commi ttee
me mber his counsel a nd advice were sought by his colleag ues and it
was always appa rent that he had the courage of his convictions and in
any controversy was ready to defend his position. When his reasoning
prevailed, as it so often did . he accepted it with humility and when he
fo und h imself outvoted, he accepted the decision with a smile.
He was born in the state of Illinois in 1889 and moved to California
wi th his family when he was less than one year old. He attended the
pu blic schools of Fresno and was a graduate of Stanford University.
In 191 2 he was a member of the graduating class of H a rvard Law
School. H e was admitted to the bar in 191 3 and practiced his chosen
profession in the city o f Fresno for the following seventeen years, taking
time o ut only to serve his country during World W ar I. A t the time
o f his discha rg e from the service he held the rank of F irst Lieutenant
in the Ai r Corps. In f 930 he became Trust Officer for the Security Bank
of Fresno and served in that capacity ui1til his retirement in 1943.
Hi s Masonic career star ted in 1922 when he beca me a M as ter M ason
in Fresno Lodge No. 247. H e v.ras M aster of his Lodge in 1928. He was
appoin ted Inspector of the district an d served during the years of 1929
and 1930. In 1934 he was chosen as an A ssistant Grand Lecturer and
held that office until his election as Grand Lecturer in 1941 . A t the
An nual Communication of this Gra nd Lodge in 1944 his brethren w isely
selected him to be their Junio r Gra nd Warden. He was elevated to the
offices of Senior Grand W arden and Deputy G rand M aste r. and at
the 1947 Communication he was elected and installed as Grand M aster
of M aso ns in California.
He became a member of the Fresno Bodies of the Scottis h Rite in
1924 and in recognition of his services. the ran k and decoration o f Knight
Commander of the Court of Honour was bestowed upon him in 1939.
In 1943 he was corone ted a Thirty-third Degree Scottish Ri te Mason .
H e found ou tlet for his bound less energies in ma ny fiel ds of endeavor. H e was a P ast P reside nt of the F resno Chamber o f Com merce,
a Rotarian, a me mber of the Ca lifornia Highwa y C o mmission for m<iny

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ANNUAL AUDIT OF RETURNS
LYBRAND. Ross BRos. &. MONTGOMERY

1.

BUSH

STREET

SAN FRANCISCO 4

Basis of Accounting:

YUKON 1·933~

The financial statements are stated.on the cash basis of
accounting. Transactions generally are recorded at the time of the
receipt or payment of cash. Current operating expense bills unpaid
were of nominal amount.
2.

Furniture and Fixtures:

Grand Lodge at the 1957 Communication approved the capitalization of amounts expended for furnishings and equipnent .after that
date. Additions during the years ended June 30, 1964 .and 19~3 amounted
to $1,924 and $2,674, respectively. Depreciation of this asset is not ·
being taken into account in the financial statements.
3 •. Insurance Premiums Adyanced for Lodges:
Comprehensive liability insurance is purchased by Grand
Lodge on a three-year basis to cover the Lodges not otherwise covered
by such insurance. Premiums are collected from the covered Lodges
on an annual premium basis.
4.

Reserve for "California Freemason":

The 1958 Communication authorized the establishment of the
Reserve for ·"California Freemason" to provide for the time when the
cash receipts, due to the prior prepayment of subscriptions, may not
equal the current expenses of publishing the magazine. The 1963
.communication appropriated $4,941 to be transferred to the Reserve
during the year ended June 30, 1964. 'lllis was the excess of cash
receipts for subscriptions over publication payments for the year
ended June 30, 1963. The Reserve amounted to $40,109 at June 30, 1964.
Approximately 337, 000 individual copies of future issues of "CaliforniaFreemason" were subscribed and paid for at June 30, 1964 at rates of
15 to 25 cents per copy.

We 'have made an examination of the 1964 Annual Returns
of the 'constituent Lodge's of GRAND LODGE, F. & A. M. OF CALIF,ORNIA,
reporting on membership and . on ·the payments due Grand Lodge in
accordance with the ·provisione of the Constitution and Ordinances
and the action taken by Grand Lodge at thP 1963 annual· communication.
our examination was made in accordance with generally accepted
auditing · standards, and accordingly included such tests of the
accounting records .•nd such other auditing procedures as we
considered necessary in the circumstances.
'!he total payments due Grand Lodge, based upon the 1964
annual returns, amount .to $1, 072, 582, as shown by the accompanying
statement. At the date of this ·report, this amount had been
collected in full and transferred to the Grand Treasurer, with
the exce'ption of a balance of $760 arising from corrections · in
the returns which was in process of adjustment at the date of this
report.

Contingent Liability: ·

Under authorization given at the 1953 Communication , Grand
Lodge is the guarantor of notes payable by California Masonic Memorial
Temple. The original amounts of these notes totaled $3, 000, 000 which
has been reduced to $779,790 at June 30, 1964.

be later restored o ut o f income to the fund when the annuiti e s no
l onger absorb the enti re income. After restoration of the princ ipal
to the original s um of $30,000, the income from the fund is to be used
for the benefi t of the residents of the Covina Harne.

Inves tments:

Inves tments in securities purchased are stated at cost.
Secu rities received b y gift or bequest or by assignment by re•ident•
of the Home at Decoto are stated at estimated market value at the
time the securities are received or at the nominal value of $1 if the
market value is unknown. In a few instances, t he carrying value of
unlisted stocks acquired by g ift or bequest has been stated at the
per share value of the underlying asset• of the company which i•
believed to be less than t he market value.

Basis of Accounting:

The financial statements are stated on a modified cash
basis of accounting. Transactions generally are recorded at the
time of the receipt or payment of cash. c urrent operating expen•e
bill• unpaid were of nominal amount.

COMMITTEE ON RITUAL
Grand Lecturer Donald G. Campbell and his six Assistant Grand
Lecturers have given us devoted and loyal assistance on every occasion
when requested. The Grand Jurisdiction of California is held in high
esteem by every Grand Lodge in North America due to the excellence
of the degree work being done by all of our constituent Lodges. My
sincere thanks to all the members of this very important Committee.
I also wish to take this occasion to thank the Inspectors of all the
Masonic Districts of this Grand Jurisdiction for their help and assistance
during my year as Grand Master. They constitute a great and hard working group of dedicated and devoted workers, and a mighty and valuable
force for every Grand Master in carrying through his program.
RESEARCH LODGES AND
COMMITTEE ON MASONIC EDUCATION
A survey of Masonic education throughout the United States.
undertaken by the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Education.
shows that virtually every grand jurisdiction has a program for Masonic
education or is planning one. Those jurisdictions with the best programs
also appear to be making the best Masonic progress.
In California the Committee on Masonic Education and the four
Research Lodges have rendered an invaluable service this past year.
Members of the Research Lodges have traveled more than 100,000 miles
at their own expense, visiting Lodges when requested to do so, and giving
talks. presenting panels or seminars. A wealth of authentic information
concerning Masonic history. symbolism and youth organizations has
been communicated in this fashion.
The Committee on Masonic Education has been of great beneflt to
Masonry in California by coordinating the efforts of the Research
Lodges. by conducting Masonic seminars in areas beyond the reach of
the Research Lodges and finally. by using the third annual joint meeting
of the Research Lodges to promote the Masonic observance of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. This celebration was held in San
FranciscoonJulyl 1 .1964. and was well attended. the theme of the all day

SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON COMMITTEE STRUCTURE
Junior Past Grand Master Ira W. Coburn. in his Annual Message
to the Grand Lodge in 1963, made the following recommendation: "I
therefore recommend that a special committee be appointed by the incoming Grand Master to make a thorough study of our present overall
committee structure, their duties. activities, objectives. etc.. with the
objective of consolidation where possible and the elimination of overlapping responsibilities."
Pursuant to this recommendation, your Grand Master appointed a
committee of five members to make this study on committee structure
and prepare its report for presentation to Grand Lodge at its Annual
Communication in October, 1964. The members of this most important
Committee are:
Theodore Meriam, Chairman
Guy B. Mize
Elbert W. Davis
Ralph H. Head
Wakefield Taylor
This Committee has held many meetings and will in due time make its
report to this Grand Communication. I urge your careful attention to this
report for the reason that it is of great importance to our Grand Lodge
committee structure.
CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
I wish at this time to compliment and commend Brother Newcomb
Candee for another year of remarkable achievement on behalf of the
California Freemason. Our Grand Lodge magazine has achieved an
outstanding position among the official Masonic publications due to the
devoted and dedicated efforts of Brother Candee. It started eleven years
ago during the term of Past Grand Master Frank Harwell, Jr. It has
Improved constantly under the editorship of Committee Chairman Newcomb Candee. It is a readable, inspirational and informative magazine.
